Implements legally compliant data retention with automated enforcement to prevent violations. Formal retention governance defines how long data must be kept (regulatory requirements) and when it must be deleted (privacy laws, data minimization). Automated enforcement ensures deletions happen on schedule without manual intervention—no "forgot to delete" violations. Legal hold capabilities freeze deletion for litigation while maintaining normal retention for other data. Consistent application across all locations prevents partial compliance where some systems delete on schedule while others accumulate data forever. Essential for GDPR (deletion requirements), HIPAA (retention requirements), and litigation readiness. Manual retention management creates gaps and violations.

Check:
• Formal retention policies documented
• Automated deletion enforcement
• Legal hold capabilities exist
• Consistent enforcement across all storage

Ask: Legal/Data Governance team

Prevents tenant isolation failures through VM-level microsegmentation. Container isolation alone is insufficient—vulnerabilities in container runtimes (Docker, containerd) or kernel exploits can allow container escapes. Kata Containers or similar VM-based isolation ensures each AI job runs in a separate virtual machine with true kernel isolation. One tenant's compromised job cannot access another tenant's memory or data—the hypervisor enforces boundaries. This also prevents access to internal corporate databases if isolation fails. Critical for multi-tenant AI platforms or shared infrastructure where jobs from different security contexts run on the same physical hardware. VM isolation provides defense-in-depth beyond container boundaries.

Check:
• VM-level isolation (Kata Containers or similar)
• Microsegmentation prevents cross-tenant access
• Corporate database access blocked from AI jobs
• Hypervisor-enforced boundaries verified

Ask: Infrastructure/Security team

Creates single point of control and visibility for all AI traffic through centralized gateway. Enterprise API Gateway enforces WAF rules (blocking attacks), DDoS mitigation (handling traffic spikes), and central logging (compliance/forensics) consistently across all models. Without centralization, each API might implement security differently (or not at all), creating gaps. Multiple gateways fragment visibility—you can't see complete traffic patterns or detect distributed attacks. Single gateway simplifies security management, policy enforcement, and incident response. All AI traffic passes through one controlled chokepoint where security controls are applied uniformly. Essential for enterprise-scale AI where consistency and visibility matter.

Check:
• Single API Gateway for all AI models
• WAF rules enforced centrally
• DDoS protection configured
• Centralized logging to SIEM

Ask: API/Security team

Protects internal microservice communication through Service Mesh encryption and routing. Service Mesh (Istio, Linkerd) enforces mTLS automatically between all services—no code changes needed. Dynamic traffic routing enables A/B testing, canary deployments, and circuit breaking. Without Service Mesh, each microservice must implement its own mTLS, creating inconsistency. The mesh provides central policy enforcement, observability, and security for east-west traffic (service-to-service) which is often neglected compared to north-south traffic (external-to-internal). Critical for complex AI architectures with many microservices where manual security implementation is error-prone. The mesh makes security automatic and consistent.

Check:
• Service Mesh deployed (Istio/Linkerd)
• mTLS automatic between all services
• Dynamic traffic routing configured
• Central policy enforcement

Ask: Infrastructure/Platform team

Protects AI workloads through comprehensive network security stack. Centralized firewalls control traffic flows, IDS/IPS detect and block attacks, flow logging provides visibility for investigations, and secure hybrid connectivity (VPN/SD-WAN) protects remote sites. Without layered defenses, single security control failures expose AI infrastructure. IDS/IPS catches attacks firewalls miss; flow logs enable forensics after breaches; VPN encrypts remote connections. AI workloads need enterprise-grade network security—model theft, data exfiltration, and infrastructure compromise are all network-based attack vectors. Comprehensive monitoring detects anomalies indicating compromise. Essential for production AI handling sensitive data or valuable intellectual property.

Check:
• Centralized firewalls protecting AI networks
• IDS/IPS monitoring AI traffic
• Flow logging to SIEM
• Secure VPN/SD-WAN for hybrid connections

Ask: Network Security team

Detects sophisticated data theft that evades traditional security through behavioral analysis. Advanced NTA tools identify "low and slow" exfiltration—small data transfers over weeks/months that don't trigger volume-based alerts. Attackers stealing training data might exfiltrate gigabytes gradually to avoid detection. Traditional tools miss this pattern. Behavioral analysis learns normal traffic patterns and flags deviations: unusual destinations, strange timing, uncommon protocols. Development environments are often less secured than production, making them exfiltration targets. AI development data (proprietary models, training sets) is extremely valuable—advanced detection is warranted. Essential for protecting intellectual property in AI research and development environments.

Check:
• NTA tools monitoring AI environments
• Behavioral analysis vs. signature-based only
• Low-and-slow pattern detection
• Alert on unusual exfiltration patterns

Ask: Network Security/SOC team

Protects sensitive training data from internet exposure through dedicated private connections. Direct Connect/ExpressRoute creates private fiber links bypassing public internet—lower latency, higher bandwidth, and no internet exposure. Training data containing PII, trade secrets, or proprietary information should never traverse public networks where it's vulnerable to interception. Private links provide guaranteed bandwidth for large dataset transfers and avoid internet congestion. Essential for hybrid AI architectures where training happens on-premises but leverages cloud resources, or vice versa. Private connectivity is more expensive but critical for security and performance of sensitive AI workloads. Alternative is encrypted VPN, but dedicated links provide better performance and isolation.

Check:
• AWS Direct Connect/Azure ExpressRoute deployed
• Dedicated private fiber connections
• No sensitive data over public internet
• Bandwidth guaranteed for AI workloads

Ask: Network/Cloud Infrastructure team

Establishes enterprise-grade identity management across AI ecosystem. Foundational IAM provides centralized authentication, authorization, and auditing. PAM secures privileged accounts (admins, developers) with additional controls. Automated provisioning/de-provisioning based on HR systems prevents orphaned accounts. Phishing-resistant MFA (hardware tokens, biometrics) blocks credential theft attacks. Without comprehensive IAM, access control is inconsistent, privileged accounts lack monitoring, and account lifecycle management is manual. AI systems often have complex access patterns—data scientists, ML engineers, automated agents—requiring sophisticated IAM. Strong authentication is critical as AI infrastructure becomes high-value attack target. Essential foundation for any enterprise AI security program.

Check:
• Centralized IAM framework deployed
• PAM for privileged access
• Automated user lifecycle management
• Phishing-resistant MFA enforced

Ask: IAM/Security team

Provides accountability and oversight for emergency administrative access through comprehensive monitoring. Break-glass accounts bypass normal controls for emergency recovery—but this power requires maximum oversight. PAM vault brokers access (creating audit trail), video recording captures everything admins do (preventing undetected malicious actions), and SOC alerting ensures security knows emergency access is active. Without these controls, break-glass becomes untraceable backdoor. Emergency access is necessary but dangerous—it must be heavily monitored. Video recording provides irrefutable evidence of actions taken. Essential for compliance (SOX, PCI) and preventing insider threats. Emergency access should be rare and always logged.

Check:
• PAM vault brokers break-glass access
• Full video recording of sessions
• Real-time SOC alerts
• Complete audit trail maintained

Ask: IAM/Security Operations team

Prevents terminated employees retaining system access through automated HR-driven revocation. 60-minute guarantee ensures departing employees (especially involuntary terminations) cannot access systems, steal data, or sabotage before access is removed. Manual processes take hours or days, creating massive risk windows. Automated HR integration triggers immediate revocation when termination is processed—no waiting for tickets. This covers SSO, cloud access, local systems, everything. Critical for insider threat prevention—highest risk period is immediately after termination notification. Without automation, terminated employees commonly retain access for days while IT processes tickets. Speed matters: 60 minutes vs 24 hours is the difference between data safe and data stolen.

Check:
• HR system integration with IAM
• Automated triggers on termination
• All access revoked within 60 minutes
• Coverage includes SSO, cloud, local systems

Ask: IAM/HR IT team

Enforces strongest authentication for highest-risk access using phishing-resistant hardware. FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware tokens cannot be phished (unlike SMS, authenticator apps, or passwords)—they use cryptographic challenge-response that only works on legitimate sites. Developers and data scientists have write access to code repositories and training data—the crown jewels. Their compromise leads directly to intellectual property theft or supply chain attacks. Password/SMS MFA is vulnerable to phishing attacks that steal credentials. Hardware token authentication eliminates this vector—attackers cannot steal what doesn't leave the token. Essential for protecting high-value assets from sophisticated phishing attacks targeting privileged users.

Check:
• FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware tokens required
• Mandatory for write-access to code/data
• No SMS or software-only MFA allowed
• Token distribution and management process

Ask: IAM/Security team

Prevents unauthorized physical access to sensitive AI infrastructure through layered physical security. Biometric dual-factor (fingerprint + badge, or iris + PIN) ensures stolen credentials alone cannot grant access. Physical caging around racks containing sensitive workloads creates additional barrier beyond data center perimeter. This protects against insider threats, social engineering, and sophisticated attacks requiring physical access. AI infrastructure often contains valuable model weights, training data on local storage, or cryptographic keys. Physical access enables drive theft, hardware tampering, or cold-boot attacks. Essential for on-premises infrastructure processing highly sensitive data. Cloud environments handle this, but colocation and hybrid environments need explicit controls.

Check:
• Dual-factor biometric authentication required
• Physical caging for sensitive AI racks
• Access logging and video surveillance
• Maintenance access controlled and monitored

Ask: Physical Security/Facilities team

Prevents data leakage from failed hardware through secure disposal procedures. GPU NVRAM and storage can retain training data, model weights, or cryptographic keys even after "deletion." Cryptographic wiping overwrites with encrypted random data making recovery impossible, or physical destruction (shredding, degaussing) ensures complete data elimination. Without tracking, failed components might be RMA'd to vendors with data intact, stolen during transit, or improperly disposed. Asset tracking ensures accountability throughout disposal lifecycle. Essential for compliance (GDPR, HIPAA requiring secure disposal) and protecting intellectual property. Decommissioned hardware is high-value target for competitors or attackers.

Check:
• Asset tracking for all failed components
• Cryptographic wipe before RMA/disposal
• Physical destruction for sensitive data
• Chain of custody documentation

Ask: IT Operations/Security team

Prevents production issues from unauthorized changes through governed change management. All configuration changes require approval, testing, and documentation before implementation. Automated drift detection identifies when production differs from approved configuration—catching manual changes, attacks, or bugs. Rollback capabilities enable quick recovery from bad changes. Without change management, "cowboy sysadmins" make undocumented changes that break systems or introduce vulnerabilities. Drift detection finds these changes immediately. Essential for maintaining stable, secure AI infrastructure where reliability and reproducibility matter. Change tracking enables root cause analysis when incidents occur. Automated enforcement prevents bypassing the process.

Check:
• Formal change management process
• Automated configuration drift detection
• Automated rollback capabilities
• All changes tracked and auditable

Ask: IT Operations/DevOps team

Ensures log integrity and non-repudiation through cryptographic proof. Blockchain or cryptographic hashing creates tamper-evident logs where any modification invalidates the hash chain. This proves logs haven't been altered—critical for forensic investigations, compliance audits, and legal proceedings. Without cryptographic proof, attackers (or insiders) can modify logs to hide their activities. Hash chains make modification detectably impossible. Real-time integrity verification catches tampering attempts immediately. Essential for regulated industries requiring provable audit trails and any high-security environment where log trustworthiness is critical. Non-repudiation means logged events cannot be denied—cryptographic proof they occurred.

Check:
• Cryptographic hashing or blockchain for logs
• Real-time integrity verification
• Tamper detection alerts
• All AI operational and training logs covered

Ask: Security/Compliance team

Enables comprehensive threat detection through unified log aggregation and correlation. SIEM ingestion of all logs—cloud flow logs, API gateway metrics, model inference logs—allows cross-stack correlation that individual systems cannot achieve. Attacks span multiple layers; seeing the complete picture enables detection. API abuse plus unusual cloud traffic plus model inference anomalies together indicate compromise; separately they might seem benign. Without aggregation, security teams investigate blind—missing patterns visible only across systems. Essential for AI infrastructure where attacks can target multiple layers simultaneously. Comprehensive visibility is foundation for effective threat hunting and incident response.

Check:
• SIEM ingests all AI-related logs
• Cloud flow logs included
• API gateway metrics aggregated
• Model inference logs correlated
• Cross-stack threat hunting enabled

Ask: Security Operations/SIEM team

Provides operational foundation for reliable AI infrastructure. Comprehensive ITOps includes incident management (responding to outages), business continuity (maintaining operations during disruptions), and configuration governance (preventing drift). Without these foundations, AI infrastructure lacks operational discipline—incidents handled ad-hoc, no disaster recovery plans, configurations drift creating instability. ITOps workflows ensure AI systems have same operational maturity as traditional IT. This includes runbooks, escalation procedures, change management, and continuous improvement. Essential for production AI where downtime has business impact. Treating AI infrastructure differently from core IT creates operational gaps and reliability problems.

Check:
• Formal incident management processes
• Business continuity plans tested
• Configuration drift governance
• ITOps workflows cover AI infrastructure

Ask: IT Operations team

Validates infrastructure resilience through intentional failure injection. Chaos Engineering experiments deliberately break components (kill servers, inject latency, corrupt data) to verify automated failover works as designed. Production environments accumulate configurations never actually tested under failure—you discover your failover doesn't work during real incidents. Chaos tests find these gaps in controlled conditions. Mathematical validation means testing proves resilience properties, not hoping they work. Essential for critical AI infrastructure where downtime is expensive. Tests should cover realistic failure scenarios: network partitions, GPU failures, database outages. Routine execution (monthly/quarterly) ensures resilience doesn't degrade as systems evolve.

Check:
• Automated Chaos Engineering framework
• Routine failure injection tests
• Production environment testing (controlled)
• Failover validation documented

Ask: SRE/Infrastructure team

Proves ransomware recovery capability through quarterly isolated restoration tests. Clean room environments physically separate from production ensure ransomware cannot spread to backup systems during testing. Quarterly frequency ensures procedures stay current and staff maintain skills. Backups without tested restoration are hope, not recovery plans—many organizations discover backup failures during actual disasters. Testing proves RTO/RPO targets are achievable and identifies gaps. Critical for AI infrastructure where model weights, training data, and configurations must be recoverable. Ransomware specifically targets backups—isolated testing ensures recovery capability survives backup compromise. Essential for business continuity and cyber insurance requirements.

Check:
• Quarterly restoration tests in isolated environment
• Physical separation from production (clean room)
• RTO/RPO validated through testing
• All critical AI systems covered

Ask: BCDR/IT Operations team

Enforces reliability through development halts when SLOs are violated. Service Level Objectives define acceptable performance/reliability; Error Budgets measure deviation. When error budget is exhausted (system has experienced maximum acceptable downtime/errors), new feature development stops and teams focus exclusively on reliability improvements. This prevents organizations from sacrificing reliability for features. Without enforcement, SLOs become aspirational metrics teams ignore. Halting development gets attention—reliability becomes non-negotiable. Essential for AI systems where downtime impacts users and business. Error budgets balance innovation with stability—you can move fast until you hit reliability limits, then must pause and fix. Google SRE principle proven effective.

Check:
• SLOs and Error Budgets defined
• Development halt triggers on violations
• Reliability engineering mandatory response
• Executive support for enforcement

Ask: SRE/Engineering Leadership team

Prevents untagged resources through automated IaC enforcement. Mandatory tags (risk level, data classification, owner, cost center) enable governance, security, and cost tracking. Auto-rejection at deployment means non-compliant resources never reach production—no cleanup needed. Without enforcement, tagging is optional and ignored, making governance impossible. You can't secure or budget resources you can't classify. IaC integration makes tagging automatic and verified—templates must include required tags or deployment fails. Essential for enterprise cloud governance where thousands of resources need classification and accountability. Tags enable policy enforcement, security controls, and cost allocation.

Check:
• Mandatory tag standards defined
• IaC auto-rejects missing tags
• Risk and data classification tags required
• Enforcement at deployment pipeline

Ask: Cloud Governance/DevOps team

Manages AI cloud spending through formal financial governance framework. Executive reporting ensures leadership sees costs and can make budget decisions. Chargeback mechanisms assign costs to teams creating financial accountability—teams spending money see their budget impact. Auto-scaling alignment with budgets prevents cost overruns from elastic expansion. Without FinOps framework, AI cloud spending is invisible until bills arrive. Chargeback creates spending discipline—teams optimize when they pay for usage. Essential for AI infrastructure where costs can spiral quickly. Formal framework includes budgets, forecasting, optimization, and accountability. CFO-level visibility ensures AI spending aligns with business value.

Check:
• Formal FinOps framework documented
• Executive-level cost reporting
• Internal chargeback to teams/departments
• Auto-scaling policies respect budgets

Ask: FinOps/Finance team

Reduces training costs through fault-tolerant spot instance architectures. Spot/preemptible VMs cost 60-90% less than on-demand but can be terminated anytime. Fault-tolerant architectures use checkpointing—when spot instances are terminated, training resumes from last checkpoint on new instances. Massive cost savings for acceptable disruption. On-demand instances waste money on interruptible workloads. Spot instances require architectural support (checkpointing, state management) but savings are enormous. Essential for cost-conscious AI training where compute is the largest expense. Not suitable for latency-sensitive inference, but perfect for batch training. Properly implemented, spot instances make training affordable at scale.

Check:
• Spot/preemptible instances for training
• Checkpoint/resume capability implemented
• Significant cost savings (>50%) documented
• Fault-tolerance validated

Ask: FinOps/Infrastructure team

Prevents DDoS attacks from causing runaway costs through hard autoscaling caps. Without caps, attackers can trigger infinite scaling during DDoS—your infrastructure automatically expands to handle attack traffic, generating massive bills. Hard caps limit maximum scale regardless of demand. This sacrifices some availability (you won't scale beyond cap) to prevent financial disaster. Soft limits can be overridden; hard caps are absolute. Essential for cost protection in elastic environments where scaling is automatic. The cap should be set above normal peak usage but well below bankruptcy-level. Prevents weaponized autoscaling where attackers use your elastic scaling against you.

Check:
• HPA hard caps configured
• Maximum scale limits absolute
• Caps prevent runaway costs
• Limits set above normal peaks

Ask: FinOps/Kubernetes team

Enables accurate cost allocation through enforced metadata tagging. Granular tags (Department, Model Version, Environment, Cost Center) allow precise chargeback—"Department X spent $50K on Model Y in Production." Without granular tags, costs are allocated by guesswork or equally divided (unfair). IaC enforcement makes tagging mandatory and correct—resources cannot deploy without required metadata. Tags enable cost optimization (identify expensive resources), governance (who owns what), and financial accountability (teams see their spending). Essential for enterprise AI where multiple teams share infrastructure and costs need fair allocation. Accurate chargeback drives spending discipline and optimization.

Check:
• Granular metadata tags defined
• IaC enforcement prevents untagged resources
• Tags include department, model, environment
• FinOps chargeback uses tag data

Ask: FinOps/Cloud Governance team

Assesses strategic risks from long-term cloud commitments before locking in. Vendor lock-in evaluation considers migration difficulty, proprietary services, data portability. Contract flexibility assesses termination clauses, price changes, commitment periods. Technology obsolescence evaluates whether current choices will be viable in 3-5 years. Without evaluation, organizations sign multi-year commitments without understanding exit costs or flexibility. Cloud AI services often use proprietary APIs and formats making migration expensive. Long-term contracts save money but reduce agility. Essential for strategic planning—understanding total cost of ownership including exit. Formal evaluation informs negotiation and architecture decisions.

Check:
• Vendor lock-in analysis performed
• Contract flexibility evaluated
• Technology obsolescence considered
• Multi-year risks formally documented

Ask: Strategy/Procurement team

Establishes organizational commitment and accountability for AI governance through executive-level ownership. Board-approved AI policy signals AI is a strategic priority requiring top-level oversight, not just an IT concern. The designated owner ensures someone is accountable for policy enforcement, updates, and compliance—preventing the policy from becoming a forgotten document. Without board approval, AI policy lacks authority and can be ignored by business units pursuing competitive advantage. Without a clear owner, responsibility diffuses across the organization and nobody drives consistent implementation. Essential for demonstrating due diligence to regulators, investors, and stakeholders.

Check:
• Board or senior management approved policy exists
• Policy has designated owner with authority
• Approval documented and dated
• Owner accountability clearly defined

Common mistake: Creating policy without designating an owner, leading to zero enforcement or accountability.

Ask: Governance/Legal team

Ensures comprehensive AI governance through complete lifecycle coverage across the entire organization. Effective AI policy must address all stages from strategy through decommissioning and apply uniformly to all entities—no subsidiaries, contractors, or geographies exempt. Partial coverage creates governance gaps where risky AI deployments slip through. If the policy only covers internal development but not third-party AI, vendors become the weak link. If it applies to headquarters but not subsidiaries, local teams deploy ungoverned AI creating enterprise-wide risk. Comprehensive coverage prevents organizational fragments from operating outside governance, ensuring consistent risk management regardless of where or how AI is developed or deployed.

Check:
• All lifecycle stages explicitly covered
• Policy applies across all business units and geographies
• Subsidiaries and contractors explicitly included
• Third-party AI usage governed

Common mistake: Writing policy that only covers internal development, ignoring third-party AI and SaaS tools.

Ask: Governance/Legal team

Transforms AI policy from aspirational document to operational reality through formal enforcement. Mechanisms like deployment approvals (can't deploy without compliance sign-off), SDLC integration (compliance checkpoints in development pipeline), audits (verification of adherence), and attestations (teams certify compliance) make policy mandatory rather than optional. Without enforcement, policy becomes "shelfware"—exists on paper but ignored in practice. Teams under deadline pressure will skip policy compliance unless it's technically or procedurally enforced. Effective enforcement means non-compliant AI systems cannot reach production, creating real accountability and consistent application of governance standards.

Check:
• Deployment approval gating enforced
• SDLC integration with compliance checkpoints
• Regular audits verify adherence
• Attestations required from teams

Common mistake: Having detailed policy with zero enforcement mechanisms, making compliance voluntary.

Ask: Governance/Compliance team

Ensures AI policy remains current with rapidly evolving technology and regulations. AI landscape changes faster than most domains—new capabilities, attack vectors, and regulations emerge continuously. Policies over 12 months old likely miss recent developments like new EU AI Act requirements, emerging attack patterns, or novel AI capabilities. Annual reviews should be minimum frequency; more frequent reviews may be warranted given regulatory velocity. Stale policies create false security—teams think they're compliant with outdated requirements while actually violating current regulations. Recent review demonstrates active governance commitment and adaptation to changing risk landscape.

Check:
• Last review date within 12 months
• Review schedule documented
• Updates reflect recent regulatory changes
• Review process includes stakeholder input

Ask: Governance/Legal team

Enables policy adaptation to regulatory changes and emerging use cases through structured update process. Formal process defines triggers (new regulations, new use cases, incidents), responsibilities (who initiates updates), approval workflows, and communication mechanisms. Without this, policy updates happen reactively and inconsistently—or not at all. When EU AI Act requirements change or the organization adopts new AI capabilities, there must be a defined path for incorporating these changes into policy. Ad-hoc updates risk missing critical changes or implementing contradictory requirements. Formal process ensures timely, coordinated policy evolution maintaining governance effectiveness as AI landscape shifts.

Check:
• Formal update process documented
• Regulatory change triggers defined
• New use case evaluation included
• Update approval workflow established

Common mistake: Treating policy as static document, failing to update as AI usage and regulations evolve.

Ask: Governance/Legal team

Creates enterprise-wide AI governance foundation through comprehensive, authoritative policy document. Board approval provides executive sponsorship and authority for policy enforcement across all departments. Distribution ensures all stakeholders know the requirements—policy locked in a drawer provides zero governance value. Cross-functional compliance requirement means engineering, legal, risk, compliance, and business units all operate under consistent standards. Without this foundation, AI governance fragments into department-specific approaches creating gaps and inconsistencies. Master policy establishes common language, requirements, and accountability framework enabling coordinated governance across the full AI lifecycle.

Check:
• Board-approved master policy exists
• Policy distributed to all relevant teams
• Cross-functional compliance mandated
• Lifecycle coverage comprehensive

Ask: Governance/Executive Leadership team

Ensures board-level visibility and accountability for AI risks through regular, documented briefings. Quarterly frequency keeps directors informed of evolving risk landscape, major incidents, and regulatory exposure requiring strategic decisions or resource allocation. Minuted briefings create accountability—board decisions and risk acceptance are documented, not just verbal discussions. Without executive visibility, boards cannot fulfill fiduciary duty to oversee significant enterprise risks. AI risks can have major business impact (regulatory fines, reputational damage, operational failures)—boards need aggregate view to make informed decisions about risk tolerance, investment, and strategic direction. Documentation supports regulatory compliance and demonstrates due diligence.

Check:
• Quarterly board briefings scheduled
• Risk posture and incidents reported
• Regulatory exposure communicated
• Briefings formally minuted

Common mistake: Providing annual or ad-hoc updates, leaving board unaware of emerging AI risks.

Ask: Governance/Board Relations team

Establishes clear accountability through documented role assignments for each AI system. Defining AI system owner (business accountability), risk owner (risk management), human oversight (decision review), and compliance roles (regulatory adherence) prevents responsibility gaps where nobody owns AI outcomes. Formal documentation and approval create enforceability—these aren't informal understandings but official assignments. Without defined roles, incidents trigger finger-pointing ("I thought compliance was handling that") and nobody clearly owns risk mitigation. For each system, stakeholders must know exactly who is accountable for what, enabling effective governance, rapid incident response, and clear escalation paths.

Check:
• Roles documented for each AI system
• System owner, risk owner assigned
• Human oversight responsibility defined
• Formal approval of assignments

Common mistake: Assuming roles are implicitly understood, leading to accountability gaps.

Ask: Governance/HR team

Enables direct risk escalation bypassing management hierarchies that might suppress concerns. Whistleblower protection ensures employees can raise severe AI risks without career retaliation—critical when management might prefer hiding problems. Direct governance committee access prevents risks from being buried in management layers before reaching decision-makers. This addresses situations where middle management might downplay risks to avoid blame or protect project timelines. Emergency stop mechanism is safety valve for catastrophic scenarios requiring immediate executive attention. Without protected escalation, severe risks may only surface after causing harm when front-line employees knew but couldn't safely report concerns.

Check:
• Emergency escalation mechanism documented
• Whistleblower protections legally enforced
• Direct governance committee access
• Bypass of standard reporting lines permitted

Ask: Governance/Legal/Ethics team

Prevents unauthorized system shutdowns through access-controlled kill-switch capabilities. Technical access controls ensure only pre-authorized governance personnel (not any engineer or operator) can execute emergency stops, preventing malicious or accidental service disruptions. Kill-switch is powerful capability—unauthorized use could halt critical AI services causing business damage. But restricted access must be rapid—authorized personnel need immediate ability to stop rogue systems without waiting for approvals. Access controls balance safety (preventing misuse) with effectiveness (enabling authorized emergency response). Technical enforcement means access cannot be bypassed through social engineering or privilege escalation.

Check:
• Access controls technically enforced
• Kill-switch limited to authorized personnel
• Authorization list maintained and current
• Access attempts logged and monitored

Ask: Security/Governance team

Ensures personnel have necessary competence before assuming AI-related responsibilities. Formal assessment evaluates technical skills, policy knowledge, and ethical awareness appropriate to the role—data scientists need different competencies than compliance reviewers. Without assessment, roles may be assigned based on availability rather than qualification, creating governance gaps. An AI system owner who doesn't understand bias risks cannot fulfill oversight responsibilities. Training alone is insufficient—assessment verifies learning actually occurred. This prevents "check-box training" where people attend sessions but gain no real competence. Assessment before assignment protects both organization and individuals from being set up to fail.

Check:
• Competence assessment process defined
• Assessment conducted before role assignment
• Skills, knowledge, and training verified
• Assessment criteria match role requirements

Common mistake: Assigning roles based on availability rather than verified competence.

Ask: HR/Training team

Accelerates incident response by automating failure routing to incident management platforms. Critical AI failures (safety violations, alignment failures) need immediate response—manual reporting introduces delays where seconds matter. Automated routing through PagerDuty, ServiceNow, or similar platforms ensures failures immediately trigger established incident response workflows with proper escalation and tracking. Bypassing manual reporting prevents failures from being downplayed, lost in email chains, or delayed by reporting hesitation. Integration with IT incident management applies mature response processes (runbooks, escalation procedures, communication protocols) to AI failures. Essential for production AI where rapid response limits damage from malfunctioning systems.

Check:
• Automated routing to incident platform configured
• AI safety/alignment failures included
• Integration tested and verified
• Manual reporting bypassed for critical events

Ask: IT Operations/AI Safety team

Prevents conflicts of interest through segregation of duties across AI lifecycle. Developers should not approve their own models for production; risk assessors should be independent from those building systems; approvers must be separate from both. Combined roles create bias toward approval—developers want their models deployed, creating pressure to minimize risks. Adequate segregation means different people with different incentives perform development, risk assessment, and approval functions. This mirrors financial controls (developers don't approve their own code for production) and prevents single points of failure. Without segregation, approval becomes rubber-stamping rather than genuine oversight.

Check:
• Development and approval roles separate
• Risk assessment independent from development
• No significant overlap between functions
• Segregation formally documented

Common mistake: Having same team develop, assess, and approve AI systems, eliminating independent oversight.

Ask: Governance/Compliance team

Establishes independent oversight through structural separation from development and business units. Separate reporting lines prevent business pressure from influencing risk decisions—risk/compliance teams can say "no" without career consequences from product leaders. Independent committees provide objective perspective unconstrained by delivery timelines or revenue targets. Second-line functions (risk management independent from first-line development) create checks and balances. Without structural independence, oversight functions become captured by business goals, losing objectivity. Independence means risk/compliance can escalate concerns, reject deployments, or mandate controls even when business units resist—protecting organization from risks development teams might accept for competitive advantage.

Check:
• Separate reporting lines from development
• Independent oversight committee exists
• Second-line risk function established
• Business pressure isolated from risk decisions

Ask: Governance/Organizational Design team

Reinforces independent oversight through enforced segregation preventing conflicts of interest. Structural independence means risk/compliance/ethics functions have separate leadership, budget, and objectives from development and product teams. Enforced segregation is technically or procedurally mandated, not just organizational chart separation—prevents business units from circumventing oversight. This actively manages conflicts where development teams want rapid deployment and oversight wants thorough vetting. Without enforcement, pressure to deliver can erode independence—risk teams may report to product leaders creating subtle (or overt) pressure to approve. Enforced segregation protects oversight personnel from retaliation and ensures objective risk assessment.

Check:
• Structural independence enforced, not advisory
• Separate leadership and budgets
• Conflicts of interest actively prevented
• Independence violations detected and addressed

Ask: Governance/Executive Leadership team

Ensures governance continuity through documented backup personnel and succession planning. Critical AI governance functions (approval authority, risk oversight, compliance validation) cannot have single points of failure—if the primary owner is unavailable during an emergency, backup personnel must be empowered to make decisions. Formal identification and documentation ensures backups understand their responsibilities and have necessary access/training. Without backups, governance stalls during absences (vacations, illness, departures) creating risk windows. This also addresses sudden personnel changes—if an AI risk owner quits, documented successors prevent governance gaps. Essential for business continuity and reliable governance operations.

Check:
• Backup personnel identified for critical roles
• Successors formally documented
• Backups trained and empowered
• Continuity plans tested

Common mistake: Creating single points of failure where only one person can approve or oversee critical AI decisions.

Ask: Governance/HR team

Enables clean forensic investigation without contaminating production environments during incidents. Pre-provisioned war room environments are isolated copies where investigators can analyze compromised model state, inspect malicious inputs, and test hypotheses without risking further production damage or evidence tampering. Automatic provisioning on incident detection ensures forensic resources are available immediately—no scrambling to set up investigation environments. Production contamination risk is real—running analysis in production might trigger additional model misbehavior or alter evidence. Isolated forensics preserve evidence integrity for regulatory investigations and legal proceedings. Essential for rapid, thorough incident investigation without operational disruption.

Check:
• Automated forensic environment provisioning
• Environments isolated from production
• Triggered on severe incident detection
• Model state analysis capabilities included

Ask: Security/Incident Response team

Prevents shadow AI by integrating policy into procurement gatekeeping. Vendors often embed AI features in software without disclosure—risk if legal/risk teams never review these capabilities. Procurement integration means any software potentially containing AI must pass policy compliance review before purchase approval. This catches SaaS tools with LLM features, analytics platforms with ML models, or automation tools with AI components. Without procurement integration, business units buy AI-enabled tools outside governance creating ungoverned AI sprawl. Legal and risk review evaluates vendor AI against policy requirements (data handling, transparency, bias testing) before organizational commitment. Essential control point for third-party AI governance.

Check:
• AI policy integrated into procurement process
• Software with AI features flagged for review
• Legal and risk sign-off required
• Bypass prevention enforced

Common mistake: Allowing business units to purchase AI-enabled SaaS tools without governance review.

Ask: Procurement/Governance team

Creates audit trail for accountability and regulatory compliance through comprehensive lifecycle documentation. Audit-defensible documentation proves who made what decisions, when, and why at every stage—from initial design choices through final decommissioning. This protects organization during regulatory audits, legal proceedings, or incident investigations by demonstrating due diligence. Without documentation, you cannot prove compliance, reconstruct decision rationale, or identify accountability when problems occur. Documentation includes approval records, risk assessments, testing results, monitoring logs, and change justifications. Maintained across lifecycle means historical decisions remain accessible even as systems evolve or personnel change. Essential for regulated industries and high-stakes AI.

Check:
• Comprehensive documentation across all lifecycle stages
• Decision approval records maintained
• Audit trail includes who/what/when/why
• Documentation retention meets regulatory requirements

Ask: Governance/Compliance team

Establishes baseline AI awareness across the organization through mandatory training with verification. Enterprise-wide training ensures all employees understand AI policy, recognize AI-related risks, and know their responsibilities—from executives to contractors. Role-specific assessments verify competency appropriate to job function (engineers need deeper technical knowledge than general staff). Without mandatory training, employees unknowingly violate policy or fail to recognize AI risks. Assessments distinguish genuine learning from attendance—people must demonstrate understanding, not just sit through presentations. Including contractors prevents governance gaps where external workers operate outside policy awareness. Essential foundation for effective AI governance.

Check:
• Mandatory training for all employees and contractors
• Role-specific competency assessments included
• Completion tracked and enforced
• Training covers policy and risk awareness

Ask: Training/HR team

Prevents security vulnerabilities through specialized pre-access training for privileged roles. Data scientists and engineers with production codebase access can introduce severe risks—insecure code, backdoors, data leaks, or vulnerable dependencies. Generic security training is insufficient for AI-specific threats (model poisoning, prompt injection, adversarial attacks). Mandatory specialized training before access ensures practitioners understand secure AI development patterns before they can harm production systems. This prevents learning security lessons through production incidents. Training covers AI-specific attack vectors, secure coding for ML, secret management, and vulnerability patterns unique to AI systems. Access gating creates technical enforcement.

Check:
• Specialized secure AI training modules exist
• Mandatory completion before production access
• Training covers AI-specific security threats
• Completion verified before access granted

Common mistake: Granting production access based on general security training, missing AI-specific vulnerabilities.

Ask: Security/Training team

Enforces training compliance through automated access revocation creating ongoing accountability. Direct linkage between training certification and network access to AI tools means expired certifications automatically trigger access removal—no manual review needed. This ensures continuous compliance rather than one-time training at hiring. Without linkage, training becomes optional after initial completion—people's certifications expire but they retain access. Automated revocation prevents expired-certification access gaps and incentivizes timely recertification. Technical enforcement is more reliable than manual processes and eliminates exceptions. Essential for maintaining security awareness currency in rapidly evolving AI risk landscape.

Check:
• Training completion linked to access controls
• Expired certifications trigger auto-revocation
• Technical enforcement, not manual
• Recertification requirements defined

Ask: IAM/Training team

Establishes systematic AI resource management through formal AIMS (AI Management System) processes. Structured process covering identification (finding all AI resources), documentation (recording details), review (assessing appropriateness), and continuous management (lifecycle oversight) prevents ad-hoc governance. Without formal processes, AI resources are discovered reactively, documented inconsistently, and reviewed irregularly—creating governance gaps. AIMS structure ensures no AI resource escapes governance attention. Covering all lifecycle stages means resources are managed from conception through retirement with defined checkpoints and responsibilities. Formal establishment and implementation means processes are approved, documented, and operationalized rather than aspirational.

Check:
• Formal AI resource management process documented
• Identification, documentation, review procedures defined
• Continuous management across lifecycle
• AIMS implementation verified

Ask: Governance/Operations team

Provides comprehensive visibility into AI estate through centralized, version-controlled inventory. Register documents all operational models, frameworks, tools, and data inputs—complete picture of organization's AI footprint. Version control tracks changes over time enabling change analysis and rollback if needed. Documentation includes critical details (name, owner, risk tier, dependencies) for governance and risk management. Centralized repository prevents scattered documentation and provides single source of truth. Covering active lifecycle stages ensures current operational systems are visible. Without comprehensive register, organizations cannot govern what they cannot see—shadow AI and ungoverned systems proliferate. Essential foundation for enterprise AI governance.

Check:
• Centralized AI system register maintained
• Version control implemented
• All operational systems documented
• Owner, risk tier, dependencies recorded

Common mistake: Maintaining decentralized or informal tracking, losing visibility into organizational AI usage.

Ask: Governance/IT Operations team

Enables traceability and risk alignment through explicit lifecycle phase mapping. Mapping AI resources to defined phases (design, development, validation, deployment, monitoring, change, decommissioning) shows where each resource is in its journey and what governance requirements apply. Different phases have different risk profiles and controls—development phase needs different oversight than production deployment. Without lifecycle mapping, resources lack context—you can't determine if a model should still be in testing or if it's inappropriately in production. Phase mapping enables phase-appropriate governance, accurate risk assessment, and identification of stalled or improperly progressed resources. Essential for lifecycle-based governance frameworks.

Check:
• AI resources mapped to lifecycle phases
• Phase definitions documented and consistent
• Mapping maintained as resources progress
• Phase-specific governance applied

Ask: Governance/Operations team

Establishes accountability and consistency for AI documentation through formal governance structure. Documented governance covering ownership (who maintains documentation), review frequency (how often updates occur), approval mechanisms (who validates changes), change management (how updates are controlled), and audit verification (how compliance is checked) ensures documentation remains accurate and current. Without governance structure, documentation degrades—becomes outdated, inconsistent, or abandoned. Formal structure assigns responsibility and creates processes preventing documentation decay. Review frequency ensures periodic validation, approval prevents unauthorized changes, and audit verification confirms compliance. Essential for maintaining documentation integrity supporting governance decisions.

Check:
• Documentation governance structure documented
• Ownership and responsibilities defined
• Review frequency and approval mechanisms established
• Change management and audit procedures defined

Ask: Governance/Documentation Management team

Prevents security risks from orphaned resources through automated decommissioning verification. When models retire, associated APIs and service accounts often remain active—creating backdoors attackers can exploit. Manual verification misses endpoints and accounts, especially in complex systems with many integrations. Automated API-discovery tools scan for all endpoints referencing the retired model, verify their destruction, and detect orphaned resources. This ensures clean decommissioning with no residual attack surface. Without automation, dormant endpoints and zombie accounts persist indefinitely, accumulating security debt. Essential for security hygiene and preventing posthumous exploitation of retired systems.

Check:
• Automated API discovery tools deployed
• Orphaned endpoint detection during decommissioning
• Service accounts associated with model verified destroyed
• Automation integrated into retirement process

Common mistake: Decommissioning models without verifying all associated endpoints are removed, leaving attack surface.

Ask: Security/DevOps team

Prevents unauthorized data usage through cryptographic enforcement of data provenance. Watermarks or metadata lineage tags mathematically prove data origin and licensing—unlicensed or unauthorized data physically cannot enter training pipeline due to technical controls. This is stronger than policy-based controls which can be bypassed. Cryptographic watermarks are tamper-evident—removing them breaks the watermark revealing manipulation. Automated enforcement means data without proper lineage is rejected automatically, no manual checks needed. Essential for copyright compliance, license management, and preventing data poisoning from untrusted sources. Protects against both inadvertent inclusion of problematic data and intentional training on unauthorized sources.

Check:
• Cryptographic watermarks or lineage tags implemented
• Mathematical enforcement, not policy-based
• Training pipeline rejects unmarked data
• Tamper detection capabilities verified

Ask: Data Governance/Engineering team

Prevents data contamination through strict categorization and version control. Segregating training vs. production data prevents production data (which may contain adversarial examples or corrupted inputs) from contaminating training sets. Version control tracks dataset evolution enabling reproducibility and rollback. Unified searchable namespace allows finding specific datasets while maintaining segregation through access controls. Without categorization, datasets blur together creating cross-contamination risks—production data with PII accidentally used for training, or outdated training data served to production. Strict segregation creates clear boundaries; version control provides accountability and reproducibility. Essential for data integrity and compliance.

Check:
• Datasets categorized by lifecycle purpose
• Physical or logical segregation enforced
• Version control for all datasets
• Unified searchable namespace implemented

Common mistake: Mixing training and production data without clear segregation, causing contamination and compliance issues.

Ask: Data Engineering/Governance team

Enforces fairness mathematically before model training through feature store validation. Demographic Parity (groups receive outcomes at equal rates) and Equalized Odds (equal false positive/negative rates across groups) are measurable fairness criteria. Measuring and enforcing these in feature store prevents biased features from reaching models—fixing bias at the source rather than trying to debias models later. Mathematical measurement provides objective fairness assessment, not subjective judgment. Enforcement means biased features are rejected automatically before model ingestion. This is preventive control rather than detective—stops bias before it becomes embedded in models. Essential for applications with fairness requirements or disparate impact concerns.

Check:
• Demographic Parity or Equalized Odds measured
• Mathematical measurement in feature store
• Enforcement prevents biased feature ingestion
• Fairness thresholds defined and validated

Ask: Data Science/Ethics team

Provides executive visibility into data quality through regular quantitative reporting. Data Quality Index (DQI) dashboard aggregates metrics like completeness, accuracy, consistency, and timeliness across all AI data sources. Monthly executive review ensures data quality is strategic priority, not just technical detail. Risk committee oversight connects data quality to enterprise risk—poor data quality leads to poor AI decisions. Without executive-level monitoring, data quality degrades invisibly until AI failures occur. Quantitative index enables trend analysis and accountability for data quality improvements. Regular review cadence prevents data quality from being neglected until crisis. Essential for data-dependent AI reliability.

Check:
• DQI dashboard tracking enterprise data health
• Monthly executive risk committee review
• Quantitative metrics across all AI data
• Trends and issues escalated

Ask: Data Governance/Executive team

Ensures permanent data destruction through cryptographic or verified methods when retention expires. Automated cryptographic shredding destroys encryption keys making data mathematically unrecoverable—simpler and more verifiable than trying to delete every copy. Verified destruction protocols provide proof data was eliminated, not just marked deleted. Without secure destruction, expired training data persists indefinitely creating compliance violations (GDPR, data minimization) and security risks (old data breaches). Automation ensures destruction happens on schedule without manual intervention that can be forgotten or skipped. Essential for regulatory compliance and reducing data exposure surface.

Check:
• Automated cryptographic shredding or verified destruction
• Triggers based on retention period expiration
• Destruction verified and logged
• Applies to all training data repositories

Ask: Data Governance/Security team

Ensures synthetic data reliability through mathematical validation against real-world ground truth. Synthetic data can inherit biases, have unrealistic distributions, or produce models that fail on real data. Formal validation measures margin of error (how much synthetic deviates from real), hallucination rate (generation of impossible patterns), and statistical validity (distribution matching). Trusted holdout set provides objective comparison—synthetic data must match real-world characteristics. Without validation, synthetic training produces models that perform well on synthetic test sets but fail in production. Mathematical validation provides quantitative confidence in synthetic data quality before expensive training investment.

Check:
• Formal mathematical validation process
• Comparison against trusted ground-truth holdout
• Margin of error and hallucination rate measured
• Statistical validity verified before training

Common mistake: Using synthetic data without validating it matches real-world distributions, producing unrealistic models.

Ask: Data Science team

Governs third-party data through comprehensive vendor management. Third-party data providers, annotation vendors, and labeling services directly impact AI quality and introduce risks (bias, quality issues, data privacy violations). Formal identification ensures all vendors are known and tracked. Assessment evaluates vendor capabilities and risks. Contractual controls establish requirements and liability. QA monitors ongoing quality. Audits verify compliance. Bias monitoring detects problematic patterns. Without this governance, third-party data is black box—you inherit their biases and quality issues unknowingly. Comprehensive vendor management extends governance beyond organizational boundaries to the full AI data supply chain.

Check:
• Third-party data vendors formally identified
• Risk assessment and contractual controls applied
• Quality assurance and audits conducted
• Bias monitoring implemented

Ask: Procurement/Data Governance team

Detects ungoverned AI through continuous automated discovery of shadow systems. Shadow AI occurs when teams deploy models outside official inventory—using unauthorized APIs, local deployments, or personal AI tools. Automated discovery tools scan networks, API gateways, and system logs for AI activity signatures. Continuous detection catches shadow AI quickly before it becomes embedded in operations. Without automated detection, shadow AI is discovered through incidents or manual reports—too late. Tools flag suspicious patterns (unusual API calls, GPU usage, model inference traffic) for investigation. Essential for comprehensive AI governance—cannot govern what you cannot detect.

Check:
• Automated discovery tools deployed
• Network scanners and API gateway analyzers
• Continuous monitoring for AI signatures
• Flagging and investigation process defined

Common mistake: Relying on self-reporting, allowing shadow AI to proliferate undetected.

Ask: IT Security/Governance team

Documents external AI dependencies for risk management and portability planning. External APIs, foundation models, and managed services create vendor dependencies requiring documentation: provider details (who), model versions (what), SLAs (performance guarantees), data processing terms (privacy/security), and exit/portability (how to migrate). Without documentation, organizations cannot assess concentration risk (over-reliance on single vendor), evaluate SLA compliance, understand data handling, or plan migrations. Version tracking is critical—provider model updates can change behavior unexpectedly. Exit planning prevents vendor lock-in. Comprehensive documentation enables informed decisions about external AI dependencies and supports third-party risk management.

Check:
• External AI services inventory maintained
• Provider details and model versions documented
• SLAs and data processing terms recorded
• Exit and portability considerations documented

Ask: Vendor Management/Governance team

Protects data transmitted to external AI through comprehensive privacy controls. External APIs and foundation model providers create data exposure risks—transmitted data might be logged, used for model training, or accessed by provider personnel. Data minimization reduces transmission to absolute necessary minimum. Anonymization removes direct identifiers. Contractual DPAs establish legal data handling requirements. Jurisdictional controls ensure data doesn't cross borders violating sovereignty laws. Without these controls, sensitive data exposure to third parties creates compliance violations and privacy risks. Layered controls (technical + contractual + jurisdictional) provide defense-in-depth for external AI data protection.

Check:
• Data minimization before external transmission
• Anonymization applied where possible
• Contractual data processing agreements in place
• Jurisdictional controls enforced

Common mistake: Sending full datasets to external APIs when only anonymized subsets are needed.

Ask: Data Privacy/Legal team

Prevents supply chain attacks through cryptographically verified software transparency. SBOMs (Software Bills of Materials) list all components, dependencies, and versions in vendor AI models. Cryptographic signatures ensure SBOMs haven't been tampered with. This enables vulnerability scanning (identifying known-bad components), license compliance (detecting incompatible licenses), and supply chain risk assessment (understanding deep dependencies). Without SBOMs, vendor AI is black box—you don't know what components contain or their vulnerabilities. Required SBOMs (not optional) creates vendor accountability and enables proactive security. Essential for supply chain security given AI model complexity and numerous dependencies.

Check:
• Cryptographically signed SBOMs required from vendors
• SBOM verification before network access
• Requirement enforced, not optional
• SBOMs used for vulnerability scanning

Ask: Security/Procurement team

Prevents legal violations through licensing compliance for AI code. Open-source libraries, frameworks, and code have varying licenses (MIT, Apache, GPL, AGPL) with different requirements and restrictions. Some licenses prohibit commercial use, require source code disclosure, or have attribution requirements. Formal evaluation before integration prevents license violations that could force code removal, require source disclosure, or create legal liability. Enforced policy means developers cannot bypass licensing review. Without evaluation, organizations unknowingly violate licenses—discovering violations during audits or legal challenges. Automated scanning can assist but human review of license compatibility is essential.

Check:
• Formal licensing policy documented
• Evaluation required before integration
• Policy enforcement prevents bypasses
• Commercial use and attribution compliance verified

Common mistake: Using open-source AI code without checking licenses, leading to compliance violations.

Ask: Legal/Engineering team

Assesses strategic risks from vendor over-dependency preventing catastrophic single points of failure. Concentration risk occurs when one vendor provides critical AI infrastructure, tooling, or models—vendor failure, service termination, or price increases severely impact operations. Lock-in risk means migration is technically or economically prohibitive—proprietary APIs, formats, or integrations trap organizations. Formal assessment quantifies these risks and informs diversification strategies or exit planning. Without assessment, organizations discover concentration risk during vendor failures or price hikes when options are limited. Assessment should consider technical dependencies, cost of migration, and business continuity impact.

Check:
• Vendor concentration formally assessed
• Lock-in risk evaluated
• Dependency on single vendors quantified
• Mitigation strategies documented

Ask: Risk Management/Strategy team

Prevents deployment failures through formal definition of computing requirements before production. CPU, GPU, memory, storage, networking, and scalability specifications must be documented and approved before deployment—ensuring infrastructure can support AI workload demands. Without defined requirements, deployments fail from resource exhaustion, unacceptable latency, or inability to scale. Formal review catches unrealistic requirements before expensive procurement. Approval ensures stakeholder alignment and budget authorization. This prevents surprises like discovering the production deployment needs 10x more GPUs than budgeted or that network bandwidth is insufficient for real-time inference.

Check:
• Computing requirements formally defined
• CPU, GPU, memory, storage, networking specified
• Scalability thresholds documented
• Requirements reviewed and approved

Common mistake: Deploying AI without understanding resource requirements, causing production failures.

Ask: Infrastructure/Engineering team

Manages hosting risks through formal evaluation of infrastructure dependencies. Identifying hosting environments (on-premises, cloud, hybrid, edge) and evaluating associated risks prevents surprises. Vendor concentration risk (single cloud provider failure impacts all AI), resilience assessment (can systems survive outages), failover evaluation (recovery capabilities), and continuity planning (disaster recovery) inform architecture and contingency decisions. Without evaluation, organizations discover hosting risks during outages when options are limited. Formal evaluation enables proactive risk mitigation through multi-cloud strategies, hybrid architectures, or enhanced resilience investments. Essential for business continuity and avoiding infrastructure single points of failure.

Check:
• Primary hosting environments identified
• Vendor concentration risk evaluated
• Resilience and failover assessed
• Business continuity risks documented

Ask: Infrastructure/Risk Management team

Ensures AI service continuity through tested resilience strategies preventing business disruption. Documented resilience strategy defines how AI services survive infrastructure failures—redundant components, failover procedures, backup systems. Testing verifies strategies actually work under failure conditions—plans that sound good but fail during real incidents are worthless. Without resilience strategy, infrastructure failures cause extended AI service outages disrupting business operations. Testing identifies gaps before real incidents—discovery during actual failures is too late. Regular testing (quarterly/annually) ensures strategies remain effective as infrastructure evolves. Essential for mission-critical AI where downtime has significant business impact.

Check:
• Resilience and failover strategy documented
• Strategy covers redundancy and recovery procedures
• Regular testing conducted
• Test results validate effectiveness

Ask: Infrastructure/BCDR team

Prevents runaway cloud costs through technical spending enforcement preventing financial disasters. FinOps guardrails with hard limits automatically prevent spending beyond defined thresholds—if costs spike from DDoS, misconfiguration, or crypto mining, the system automatically stops further spending. Without hard limits, alerts notify humans but damage continues until manual intervention. Hard limits may sacrifice availability but prevent bankruptcy-level bills. Essential for cloud AI where costs can escalate rapidly—single misconfigured auto-scaling policy can generate six-figure bills overnight. Technical enforcement is faster and more reliable than manual processes during unforeseen spikes.

Check:
• Automated FinOps guardrails configured
• Hard spending limits technically enforced
• Automatic prevention of runaway costs
• Limits defined based on budget thresholds

Common mistake: Having cost alerts without hard limits, allowing catastrophic spending before human response.

Ask: FinOps/Infrastructure team

Aligns AI infrastructure with corporate sustainability commitments through continuous environmental monitoring. Measuring energy consumption, water usage (for cooling), and carbon emissions from major AI workloads enables informed decisions about environmental impact. Formal reporting provides transparency for ESG stakeholders. Explicit evaluation against sustainability targets before workload approval means environmental considerations influence AI deployment decisions—not afterthoughts. Without measurement and evaluation, organizations cannot manage AI environmental impact or demonstrate ESG progress. Continuous monitoring catches efficiency degradation over time. Essential for organizations with sustainability commitments and increasing regulatory ESG disclosure requirements.

Check:
• Environmental impacts continuously measured
• Energy, water, carbon emissions tracked
• Formal reporting to stakeholders
• Evaluation against ESG targets before approval

Ask: ESG/Infrastructure team

Prevents orphaned access through automated privilege revocation on ownership changes. When AI system owners or risk validators change roles or leave, automated triggers immediately revoke their deployment and administrative privileges—preventing unauthorized access from ex-employees or personnel who no longer have oversight responsibility. Without automation, manual revocation lags creating security windows. Role changes (internal transfers) are often overlooked compared to departures. Automated triggers based on HR system integration ensure access revocation happens within minutes of role change regardless of reason. Essential for preventing insider threats and maintaining governance accountability when personnel change.

Check:
• Automated access control triggers configured
• Revocation on role change or departure
• HR system integration for triggers
• Deployment and admin privileges covered

Ask: IAM/HR IT team

Ensures governance effectiveness through adequate staffing preventing function failures from under-resourcing. AI governance requires personnel across multiple functions—development (building systems), risk assessment (evaluating risks), validation (testing and quality), monitoring (ongoing oversight), and oversight (governance coordination). Insufficient personnel creates governance gaps where critical functions are neglected or performed inadequately. Formal assignment ensures responsibilities are clearly allocated and resourced. Without sufficient staff, governance becomes aspirational—policies exist but lack personnel to implement them. Coverage assessment identifies gaps enabling hiring or reallocation decisions before governance failures occur.

Check:
• Personnel needs for all governance functions assessed
• Sufficient staff formally assigned
• Coverage gaps identified and addressed
• Responsibilities clearly allocated

Common mistake: Creating elaborate governance frameworks without staffing them, leading to paper compliance only.

Ask: Governance/HR team

Prevents HITL approval tampering through cryptographic protection of approval logs. Human-in-the-loop approvals for high-stakes decisions (loans, medical diagnoses, legal actions) must have tamper-proof audit trails. Cryptographic hashing or blockchain creates immutable logs—alterations are detectable. Secure centralization prevents logs from being deleted locally. This protects against retroactive approval fabrication ("we approved this decision" when they didn't), approval deletion (hiding rejected decisions), or unauthorized modification (changing approval conditions). Essential for regulatory compliance, legal liability, and governance accountability. Immutable logs provide court-defensible proof of human oversight and decision-making.

Check:
• HITL approval logs cryptographically protected
• Centralized secure storage
• Tampering detection capabilities
• High-stakes decision approvals covered

Ask: Security/Governance team

Prevents competency gap risks through automated external resource funding. When internal workforce lacks skills to govern high-risk AI systems and gaps cannot be remediated before scheduled deployment, automated funding triggers engage external consultants. This prevents deploying high-risk systems without adequate oversight due to internal skill limitations. Manual processes might defer external help due to budget friction or procurement delays—automation removes barriers ensuring critical gaps are filled. Funding trigger is safety mechanism acknowledging that some deployments require external expertise and budget concerns should not compromise governance. Essential for high-risk systems where competency gaps create unacceptable risks.

Check:
• Automated funding triggers configured
• Triggered by competency gap + deployment timeline conflict
• External consultant engagement automated
• High-risk systems specifically covered

Ask: Governance/Finance team

Addresses governance skill gaps through systematic assessment and remediation. Formal competency assessment identifies specific AI-related skill gaps across governance functions (technical understanding, regulatory knowledge, ethics awareness). Documented remediation plan might include training programs, external hiring, or consultant engagement. Without assessment, organizations operate blind to competency gaps—discovering deficiencies during incidents when it's too late. Active implementation means plans are executed, not just documented. This ensures governance personnel have capabilities needed for effective oversight. Regular reassessment ensures competencies keep pace with evolving AI landscape.

Check:
• Formal competency assessment conducted
• Skill gaps identified and documented
• Remediation plan implemented (training/hiring/consultants)
• Progress tracked and verified

Ask: Governance/HR team

Extends governance to external workforce through formal documentation and oversight. External contractors, consultants, offshore teams, and managed service providers often perform significant AI work but may operate outside governance if undocumented. Formal inclusion in resource documentation with defined roles, responsibilities, and oversight controls ensures external workers follow same governance standards as internal staff. Without inclusion, external workers become governance blind spots—their activities undocumented and risks unmanaged. Controls might include contractual requirements, access restrictions, or oversight procedures. Essential for comprehensive governance when external workers are significant portion of AI workforce.

Check:
• External AI workers formally documented
• Roles and responsibilities defined
• Oversight controls established
• Contractors, consultants, offshore teams included

Common mistake: Governing internal employees while external contractors operate without oversight.

Ask: Procurement/Governance team

Prevents unauthorized changes through comprehensive change management across AI stack. Changes to models, datasets, infrastructure, tooling, or vendors can introduce risks—broken functionality, degraded performance, security vulnerabilities, or compliance violations. Formal change management requires version control (tracking changes), impact assessment (understanding risks), validation testing (verifying changes work), and documented approval (authorizing changes). Without change management, changes happen ad-hoc creating instability and untracked risk introduction. This mirrors IT change management best practices applied to AI systems. Comprehensive coverage means no component escapes governance—including external provider changes that might affect your systems.

Check:
• Formal change management process documented
• All AI components covered (models/data/infra/tools/vendors)
• Version control, impact assessment, testing, approval required
• Process enforcement verified

Ask: Change Management/DevOps team

Prevents deployment of unvetted AI through mandatory impact assessment process. Formal process ensures all in-scope AI systems undergo structured evaluation before deployment—identifying risks, impacts, and required mitigations. Without mandatory assessment, teams deploy systems without understanding potential harms or compliance implications. Formal establishment means process is officially approved and documented. Implementation means process is actually followed, not just policy. This prevents "move fast and break things" culture from deploying harmful AI. Assessment process should be proportionate—higher-risk systems get deeper assessment but all systems get some level of evaluation.

Check:
• Formal impact assessment process established
• Mandatory for all in-scope AI before deployment
• Process documented and approved
• Implementation verified and enforced

Ask: Governance/Risk team

Enforces impact assessment completion through automated deployment gating. Workflow tools create technical barriers—systems cannot promote to production without completed, approved impact assessment. Cryptographic signing or formal logging provides tamper-proof approval evidence. Hard gating means bypass is technically impossible, not just policy-prohibited. Without automation, approval requirements can be skipped under deadline pressure. Technical enforcement removes human judgment from compliance—systems either have approved assessments or cannot deploy, period. Essential for ensuring impact assessments aren't just documentation exercises but actual deployment prerequisites with teeth.

Check:
• Automated workflow management for deployments
• Hard gates prevent production promotion without assessment
• Cryptographic signing or formal logging of approvals
• Technical enforcement, not manual processes

Common mistake: Requiring impact assessments through policy but allowing deployments to bypass them under pressure.

Ask: DevOps/Governance team

Enables risk-based governance through consistent impact categorization across all systems. Formal categorization by severity levels (low, medium, high) with documented criteria ensures consistent risk classification—preventing arbitrary or politically-influenced categorization. Identified impact categories (harm, bias, privacy, safety, regulatory) provide structured evaluation framework. Without consistent categorization, low-risk and high-risk systems receive same oversight (wasteful) or high-risk systems are labeled low-risk to avoid scrutiny (dangerous).
