Documented criteria enable objective, repeatable classification supporting proportionate governance where oversight intensity matches actual risk.

Check:
• Formal categorization by severity levels defined
• Documented criteria applied consistently
• Impact categories explicitly identified
• All in-scope systems categorized

Ask: Risk Management/Governance team

Ensures human-centered risk evaluation through comprehensive harm assessment. Explicit evaluation of potential harm to individuals—including disproportionate impacts on vulnerable populations—prevents deploying systems that harm protected groups. Coverage includes discrimination (unfair treatment), financial harm (economic damage), safety risks (physical harm), and psychological harm (emotional damage). Formally identifying affected stakeholder groups ensures all impacted parties are considered, not just primary users. Without comprehensive harm assessment, organizations deploy systems causing real-world harm they didn't anticipate or consider. Essential for ethical AI and avoiding disparate impact on vulnerable populations.

Check:
• Potential individual harm explicitly evaluated
• Disproportionate impacts on vulnerable groups assessed
• Harm types: discrimination, financial, safety, psychological
• All affected stakeholder groups identified

Ask: Ethics/Risk team

Evaluates broad consequences through comprehensive downstream impact assessment. AI systems create ripple effects beyond immediate users—societal impacts (employment changes, social dynamics), economic impacts (market disruption, wealth concentration), environmental impacts (resource consumption, waste), systemic impacts (infrastructure dependencies, cascade failures), and long-term impacts (irreversible changes, future consequences). Without evaluation, organizations focus narrowly on immediate functionality while creating unintended broader consequences. Documentation provides accountability and informs mitigation strategies. Essential for responsible AI deployment considering full impact spectrum, not just technical performance.

Check:
• Societal, economic, environmental impacts evaluated
• Systemic and long-term consequences assessed
• Downstream impacts documented
• Evaluation covers broad impact categories

Ask: Strategy/Risk/Ethics team

Protects against high-impact AI failures through enhanced safeguard implementation. High-impact systems (affecting many people, high-stakes decisions, safety-critical) require additional protections beyond basic controls. Human oversight ensures human judgment in critical decisions. Bias testing detects discriminatory patterns. Privacy controls protect sensitive data. Explainability enables understanding and contestation of decisions. Monitoring alerts detect anomalies. Kill-switch enables emergency shutdown. Without enhanced safeguards, high-impact systems deploy with same controls as low-risk systems—inadequate risk mitigation. Formal definition and implementation ensures protections match risk level.

Check:
• High-impact systems formally identified
• Enhanced safeguards defined for each system
• Human oversight, bias testing, privacy controls implemented
• Explainability, monitoring, kill-switch capabilities deployed

Ask: Risk/Engineering team

Ensures informed risk acceptance through formal residual risk documentation. Post-mitigation risks that remain (residual risks) must be documented, approved by authorized decision-makers, and assessed against risk tolerance. This creates accountability—someone explicitly accepts remaining risks rather than implicitly deploying without risk understanding. Overall residual risk rating enables portfolio-level risk management. Without formal documentation, organizations don't know their actual risk exposure after controls are applied. Authorization prevents unauthorized risk acceptance. Risk tolerance comparison ensures residual risks fall within acceptable bounds. Essential for informed risk management and executive accountability.

Check:
• Residual risks formally documented post-mitigation
• Authorized decision-maker approval required
• Risk tolerance assessment conducted
• Overall residual risk rating assigned

Ask: Risk Management team

Maintains assessment accuracy through periodic and event-triggered reviews. Periodic reviews (quarterly, annually) ensure assessments reflect current system state and risk landscape. Event-triggered reassessment (model changes, incidents, new regulations, performance issues, complaints) catches significant changes requiring updated evaluation. Without reviews, assessments become outdated—systems evolve but assessments remain static. This creates false confidence in stale risk understanding. Combined periodic and event-triggered approach balances regular updates with responsive assessment when significant changes occur. Essential for maintaining assessment relevance over system lifetime.

Check:
• Periodic review schedule defined and followed
• Event triggers for reassessment documented
• Triggers include: changes, incidents, regulations, degradation, complaints
• Reassessment process enforced

Ask: Risk Management/Governance team

Integrates AI risks into enterprise risk management for holistic organizational visibility. AI impact assessments identify risks, but integration into risk register and ERM processes ensures these risks are managed alongside other enterprise risks. This enables portfolio-level risk aggregation, resource allocation based on comparative risk, and executive visibility into AI risk in broader context. Without integration, AI risks are managed in isolation potentially missing interactions with other business risks. Formal integration ensures AI risks receive appropriate attention in enterprise risk discussions and decision-making. Essential for mature risk management treating AI risks as first-class enterprise concerns.

Check:
• Impact outcomes integrated into AI risk register
• AI risks included in enterprise risk management
• Risk aggregation and portfolio view enabled
• Executive visibility through ERM processes

Ask: Enterprise Risk Management team

Maintains assessment integrity through controlled documentation repository. Version control tracks assessment evolution over time. Ownership assignment ensures accountability for accuracy. Retention periods define how long assessments are kept for compliance and audit. Audit traceability enables verification of assessment completeness and accuracy. Without controlled repository, assessments scatter across systems, versions conflict, and historical assessments are lost. Centralized control ensures single source of truth for assessment documentation supporting compliance audits and governance verification. Essential for regulatory compliance and audit-defensible governance.

Check:
• Controlled repository for assessments maintained
• Version control tracking changes
• Ownership and retention periods defined
• Audit traceability capabilities implemented

Ask: Governance/Documentation Management team

Incorporates affected voices through stakeholder engagement during assessments. Formal identification and consultation with affected stakeholders—including vulnerable populations disproportionately impacted—ensures AI development reflects real-world concerns, not just developer assumptions. High-impact systems especially benefit from stakeholder input revealing risks developers might miss. Without consultation, assessments make assumptions about stakeholder needs and harms that may be incorrect. Engagement builds trust, improves system design, and identifies mitigation strategies. Essential for ethical AI development and avoiding unintended harms to affected communities.

Check:
• Affected stakeholders formally identified
• Consultation or engagement conducted
• Vulnerable populations specifically included
• Engagement emphasized for high-impact systems

Common mistake: Making assumptions about stakeholder impacts without actually consulting affected communities.

Ask: Ethics/Stakeholder Engagement team

Improves future assessments through systematic learning from operational experience. Analyzing incident learnings, complaints, user feedback, and adverse outcomes identifies where original assessments missed risks or underestimated impacts. Systematic incorporation means lessons flow back into assessment processes—similar future systems benefit from accumulated knowledge. Without learning incorporation, organizations repeat mistakes across systems. Analysis identifies patterns (certain risk types consistently underestimated, specific stakeholder concerns frequently overlooked) enabling process improvements. Essential for continuous improvement transforming incidents and complaints into better future risk assessment.

Check:
• Systematic analysis of incidents, complaints, feedback
• Learnings incorporated into future assessments
• Pattern identification and process improvements
• Feedback loop from operations to assessment

Ask: Risk Management/Continuous Improvement team

Validates assessment accuracy through comparison with actual operational impacts. Formal comparison between predicted impacts (from assessment) and observed impacts (from deployment) identifies assessment errors—underestimated harms, overestimated benefits, missed risks. Detection process finds material discrepancies triggering investigation and response. Without comparison, assessment accuracy is never validated—organizations don't know if their assessment process actually predicts real-world impacts. Response process addresses discrepancies (system modifications, enhanced monitoring, stakeholder notification). Essential for improving assessment methodology and detecting assessment blind spots before they cause broader harm.

Check:
• Formal comparison process between predicted and actual impacts
• Material discrepancies identified and investigated
• Defined detection and response procedures
• Feedback improves assessment methodology

Ask: Risk Management/Operations team

Improves vulnerable population identification through automated tools with validation. Third-party demographic proxies or AI tools can identify vulnerable populations in datasets or user bases. However, proxy methods have error rates—demographic inference from names, locations, or behaviors is imperfect. Formal validation of margin of error ensures organizations understand confidence levels in vulnerability identification. Without validation, organizations make protection decisions based on potentially inaccurate demographic proxies. Understanding error rates informs appropriate use—high-accuracy proxies enable automated protections, low-accuracy requires human review. Essential for protecting vulnerable populations without over-relying on imperfect tools.

Check:
• Automated tools or demographic proxies utilized
• Vulnerable population identification capabilities
• Margin of error formally validated
• Accuracy understood and documented

Ask: Data Science/Ethics team

Assesses organizational consequences through comprehensive business impact evaluation. AI system failures create impacts beyond affected individuals—reputational damage (brand harm, customer trust loss), financial consequences (fines, liability, revenue loss), legal exposure (lawsuits, regulatory action), operational disruption (service outages, workflow failures), and business continuity risks (inability to operate). Without business impact assessment, organizations focus on technical risks while underestimating organizational consequences. Formal assessment informs risk acceptance decisions, insurance needs, and contingency planning. Essential for business-aligned risk management considering full organizational impact spectrum.

Check:
• Reputational, financial, legal impacts assessed
• Operational and business continuity risks evaluated
• Comprehensive business impact documentation
• Assessment informs risk management decisions

Ask: Risk Management/Business Strategy team

Ensures multi-jurisdictional compliance through region-specific impact evaluation. AI systems operating across borders face varying legal and regulatory requirements—GDPR in EU, AI Act in EU, state laws in US, sector-specific regulations. Region-specific evaluation identifies applicable requirements per jurisdiction. Documentation enables compliance verification and supports regulatory reporting. Without jurisdictional assessment, organizations unknowingly violate foreign regulations or fail to implement required protections. This is critical for global AI deployment where one-size-fits-all compliance is inadequate. Assessment should cover data protection, AI-specific regulations, and sector requirements per geography.

Check:
• Multi-jurisdictional operation identified
• Region-specific legal and regulatory impacts evaluated
• Compliance requirements documented per jurisdiction
• Assessment covers data protection and AI-specific regulations

Ask: Legal/Compliance team

Enforces jurisdictional compliance through technical controls preventing violations. Automated geofencing restricts data or AI service access by geography. Dynamic routing directs requests to compliant infrastructure per jurisdiction. Attribute-based access controls (ABAC) enforce different permissions based on user location or data origin. Technical enforcement prevents compliance violations even if applications have bugs or misconfigurations. Manual compliance processes fail—developers forget regional differences or misimplement restrictions. Automated controls mathematically guarantee compliance with data sovereignty and processing restrictions. Essential for multi-jurisdictional AI ensuring regulatory compliance through infrastructure-level enforcement.

Check:
• Automated geofencing or dynamic routing enforced
• ABAC for jurisdiction-specific access controls
• Technical enforcement of data sovereignty
• Infrastructure-level compliance guarantees

Common mistake: Relying on application-level compliance that can be bypassed through bugs or misconfigurations.

Ask: Infrastructure/Compliance team

Provides real-time transparency through auto-generated system cards explaining current AI state. Dynamic "Nutrition Labels" or System Cards show users exactly which model version, context window size, and data recency they're interacting with at that moment. Unlike static documentation that becomes outdated, automated generation ensures accuracy. This transparency enables informed user decisions—users know if they're using latest model or older version, understand context limitations, and see data freshness. Without dynamic transparency, users make assumptions about system capabilities that may be wrong. Essential for user trust and informed consent when interacting with AI systems.

Check:
• System cards or nutrition labels auto-generated
• Real-time display via UI
• Model version, context window, data recency shown
• Dynamically updated, not static

Ask: Product/Engineering team

Prevents inappropriate changes from bypassing governance through automated threshold enforcement. Materiality thresholds define when changes (model updates, dataset modifications, deployment changes) are significant enough to require reassessment or approval—preventing minor tweaks from accumulating into major risk changes. Encoding thresholds into CI/CD pipelines creates technical enforcement—significant changes automatically trigger governance workflows and cannot deploy without approval. Without thresholds, every change gets same treatment (wasteful) or significant changes slip through (dangerous). Automation ensures consistency and prevents "just a small change" excuses that bypass governance. Essential for efficient yet comprehensive change control.

Check:
• Materiality thresholds formally defined
• Thresholds encoded into CI/CD pipelines
• Automated governance triggering on threshold breach
• Model, dataset, deployment changes covered

Common mistake: Defining thresholds but not automating enforcement, allowing teams to bypass governance under deadline pressure.

Ask: Governance/DevOps team

Enforces lifecycle rigor through mandatory stage-gate requirements preventing premature progression. Entry criteria define what must be completed before entering a stage; exit criteria define what must be achieved before advancing. Mandatory evidence artifacts provide proof of completion. Without enforcement, teams skip stages or proceed without completing required activities. This mirrors manufacturing quality gates—products don't advance until requirements are met. Preventing progression without completion ensures each stage's governance value is realized. Essential for maintaining lifecycle integrity and preventing shortcuts that introduce risks.

Check:
• Entry and exit criteria formally defined per stage
• Mandatory evidence artifacts specified
• Progression blocked without completion
• Enforcement technically or procedurally mandated

Ask: Governance/Program Management team

Manages legitimate exceptions while maintaining accountability and oversight. Exceptions are sometimes necessary (emergencies, business-critical situations), but uncontrolled exceptions undermine governance. Formal protocols define when exceptions are permitted, who can approve them, documentation requirements, and post-hoc review to verify exceptions were justified. Without protocols, exceptions become routine workarounds rendering governance meaningless. Documentation creates accountability—exception approvers must justify decisions. Post-hoc review ensures exceptions were truly necessary and identifies patterns suggesting governance adjustments needed. Essential for flexible yet controlled governance.

Check:
• Exception protocols formally documented
• Approval authority clearly defined
• Rationale documentation required
• Post-hoc review process established

Common mistake: Allowing informal exceptions that become the norm, rendering formal lifecycle controls meaningless.

Ask: Governance/Compliance team

Establishes clear accountability through comprehensive role assignment across full lifecycle. Each role has specific responsibilities—lifecycle owner (overall accountability), development lead (building), independent validator (checking), risk owner (managing risks), deployment approver (production authorization), monitoring owner (ongoing oversight), retirement authority (decommissioning). Without formal assignment, responsibility diffuses and nobody owns outcomes. Documented reporting lines enable escalation; decision rights clarify who makes what decisions. Comprehensive coverage across lifecycle prevents gaps where critical functions lack assigned ownership. Essential for governance accountability and effective lifecycle management.

Check:
• All roles formally assigned per AI system
• Lifecycle owner through retirement authority covered
• Reporting lines and decision rights documented
• Assignments maintained and current

Ask: Governance/HR team

Prevents training on biased or unrepresentative data through automated quality enforcement. Circuit breakers instantly halt training pipelines when data quality issues exceed thresholds—sampling bias (data doesn't represent population), representational coverage gaps (missing critical groups). Without circuit breakers, training continues on flawed data producing biased models. Automated enforcement means data quality checks cannot be bypassed or ignored. Predefined tolerance thresholds define acceptable quality levels. Instant halting prevents wasting compute resources on data that will produce unreliable models. Essential for data quality assurance and preventing bias from entering models at source.

Check:
• Automated data quality circuit breakers implemented
• Sampling bias detection configured
• Coverage gap detection implemented
• Tolerance thresholds predefined

Ask: Data Engineering/ML Engineering team

Prevents feature engineering from introducing or amplifying bias through independent oversight. Features and transformations can create proxy discrimination (using zip code as race proxy), amplify existing biases, or accidentally delete minority group data during aggregation. Independent review provides external perspective unconstrained by development team's assumptions. Automated fairness audits mathematically measure bias in engineered features. Without independent review, developers miss their own blind spots. Feature engineering is critical stage where bias often enters—controlling this prevents downstream model bias. Essential for fair AI and regulatory compliance.

Check:
• Feature engineering independently reviewed
• Automated fairness audits conducted
• Proxy variable risks assessed
• Minority group data preservation verified

Common mistake: Allowing developers to review their own feature engineering, missing proxy discrimination and bias amplification.

Ask: Data Science/Ethics team

Enables audit reconstruction through comprehensive version control of all model components. Full reproducibility means any deployed model can be recreated exactly—critical for regulatory audits, incident investigation, or compliance verification. Components include training datasets (exact data used), code (processing and training scripts), hyperparameters (model settings), feature configurations (which features used), environment dependencies (libraries and versions), and infrastructure (compute configuration). Without reproducibility, you cannot prove what was deployed or reconstruct models for investigation. Version control provides audit trail of all changes. Essential for regulatory compliance and forensic capability.

Check:
• Training datasets version-controlled
• Code, hyperparameters, features version-controlled
• Environment and infrastructure dependencies tracked
• Full model reconstruction capability verified

Ask: ML Engineering/DevOps team

Provides objective quality assurance through structural separation of validation from development. Independent validators are separate from development team—preventing conflicts of interest where developers validate their own work. High-risk systems require external validation (separate risk function or third party) for maximum objectivity. Without independence, validation becomes rubber-stamping—validators have incentive to approve to meet timelines. Structural separation means different reporting lines and incentives. Independent validation catches issues development team might miss or minimize. Essential for objective pre-deployment quality assurance.

Check:
• Independent validation required pre-deployment
• Validators structurally separate from development
• High-risk systems validated by separate function or external party
• Independence verified and maintained

Common mistake: Having development team validate their own work, eliminating independent quality assurance.

Ask: Governance/Quality Assurance team

Prevents production compromise through comprehensive MLOps security controls. Environment segregation (dev/test/prod) prevents development issues from affecting production. Role-based access controls limit who can perform sensitive actions. Deployment approval workflows gate production changes. Immutable logging provides audit trails. Rollback capability enables quick recovery from bad deployments. Production promotion restrictions prevent unauthorized deployment. Without these controls, MLOps becomes security vulnerability—anyone can deploy anything, changes lack accountability, and rollback is manual. Comprehensive controls create defense-in-depth for ML operations. Essential for production AI security and reliability.

Check:
• Strict environment segregation enforced
• Role-based access controls implemented
• Deployment approvals and immutable logging
• Rollback capability and promotion restrictions

Ask: MLOps/Security team

Detects model degradation and bias through continuous automated monitoring. Live monitoring tracks input drift (data characteristics changing), distribution shifts (statistical properties changing), performance degradation (accuracy declining), and bias signals (discriminatory patterns emerging). Automated alerts trigger when issues detected—human monitoring cannot catch real-time problems. Escalation protocols ensure appropriate response based on severity. Without continuous monitoring, models degrade silently until user complaints or incidents occur. Real-time detection enables proactive intervention before significant harm. Essential for production AI quality and fairness maintenance.

Check:
• Continuous monitoring for drift and degradation
• Input drift and distribution shift detection
• Performance and bias signal monitoring
• Automated alerts with escalation protocols

Ask: ML Engineering/Operations team

Ensures consistent response to monitoring alerts through documented thresholds and interventions. Quantitative thresholds define acceptable deviation levels—when metrics exceed thresholds, action is required. Explicit intervention actions (rollback, suspension, retraining) are predefined not ad-hoc. Scheduled recalibration prevents threshold decay as environment changes. Without documented thresholds, intervention decisions are subjective and inconsistent. Alert tuning ensures thresholds remain meaningful—too sensitive causes alert fatigue, too lenient misses real issues. Automated interventions remove human delay from critical responses. Essential for reliable and consistent monitoring response.

Check:
• Quantitative thresholds formally documented
• Intervention actions predefined per threshold
• Scheduled alert-tuning recalibrations
• Automated interventions configured

Ask: ML Engineering/Operations team

Provides human control over high-stakes AI through formal oversight with accountability. Human oversight roles grant authority to intervene (modify AI decisions), override (reverse AI recommendations), or suspend (halt AI operations). Documentary authority ensures legal and organizational backing for interventions. Systematic logging creates audit trail of all interventions—who intervened, when, why, and what action taken. Without formal roles, interventions are ad-hoc and unaccountable. High-stakes systems (affecting rights, safety, finances) require human judgment capability. Logging enables review of intervention patterns and oversight effectiveness. Essential for accountable human control.

Check:
• Oversight roles formally defined for high-stakes systems
• Intervention, override, suspension authority granted
• All interventions systematically logged
• Audit trail maintained

Ask: Governance/Operations team

Prevents automated retraining from introducing risks through comprehensive validation gating. Retraining events change model behavior—without governance, automated retraining can introduce bias, degrade performance, or violate compliance. Data provenance and quality validation ensures training data is trustworthy. Impact reassessment evaluates whether retraining changes risk profile. Formal approval gates production promotion. Without governance, automated retraining becomes uncontrolled model modification. Validation checkpoints ensure retrained models meet quality and compliance standards before deployment. Essential for safe automated retraining.

Check:
• Data provenance and quality validation required
• Impact reassessment triggers defined
• Formal approval before production promotion
• Governance applied to all retraining events

Common mistake: Automating retraining without governance, allowing models to change behavior without validation or approval.

Ask: ML Engineering/Governance team

Ensures appropriate risk management through formal classification with regulatory awareness. AI system classification (High-Risk, Regulated, GenAI) determines governance intensity. Documented criteria enable consistent classification. Formal approval prevents arbitrary classification. Periodic independent review ensures classifications remain current as systems evolve. Regulatory horizon scanning identifies upcoming requirements triggering reassessment. Without formal classification, systems receive inappropriate oversight—high-risk systems under-governed or low-risk over-governed. Horizon scanning prevents surprise regulatory compliance failures. Classification with monitoring enables adaptive governance responding to regulatory changes.

Check:
• Classification criteria documented and approved
• Periodic independent classification review
• Regulatory horizon scanning process established
• Regulatory changes trigger reassessment

Ask: Governance/Legal/Compliance team

Provides enhanced protection for high-risk systems through proportionate governance intensification. High-risk systems (affecting many people, high-stakes decisions) warrant enhanced controls beyond basic governance. Executive approval ensures senior awareness and accountability. Extended validation scope catches more issues. Stricter intervention thresholds enable earlier response. Documented oversight creates accountability. Formal impact reassessment ensures ongoing appropriateness. Without enhanced controls, high-risk and low-risk systems receive same governance—inadequate for high-risk. Proportionate governance allocates resources based on actual risk.

Check:
• Executive approval required for high-risk systems
• Extended validation scope applied
• Stricter intervention thresholds set
• Formal impact reassessment gating enforced

Ask: Governance/Risk Management team

Ensures deployment readiness through mandatory technical documentation with governance verification. Documentation artifacts (model cards, system cards, datasheets, architecture diagrams, risk docs) capture critical information for governance and operations. Mandatory as lifecycle deliverables means documentation isn't optional. Governance sign-off confirms presence and completeness before production—incomplete documentation blocks deployment. Without mandatory documentation, systems deploy without adequate information for oversight, operations, or incident response. Sign-off creates accountability for documentation quality. Essential for governance effectiveness and operational readiness.

Check:
• Documentation artifacts formally required
• Model cards, system cards, datasheets, diagrams, risk docs
• Governance sign-off before production deployment
• Completeness verification enforced

Common mistake: Treating documentation as optional, deploying systems without adequate information for oversight.

Ask: Governance/Documentation team

Prevents external AI risks through comprehensive pre-deployment due diligence. External models (third-party, open-source) introduce supply chain risks—unknown training data, usage restrictions, licensing constraints, undisclosed limitations. Formal due diligence assesses these risks before deployment. Data provenance evaluation identifies training data issues. Usage restrictions assessment prevents license violations. Licensing constraint review ensures compliance. Limitation identification informs appropriate use. Without due diligence, organizations deploy external models blindly, inheriting unknown risks. Documentation enables informed risk acceptance decisions. Essential for third-party AI risk management.

Check:
• Formal due diligence process defined
• Data provenance assessed
• Usage restrictions and licensing evaluated
• Model limitations documented

Ask: Procurement/Risk Management team

Manages vendor model update risks through formal impact assessment before adoption. Third-party and foundation model updates can introduce breaking changes, performance regressions, safety issues, or compliance violations. Formal assessment before continued production use evaluates changes comprehensively—performance impacts, safety implications, compliance obligations, contractual risk. Documented approval creates accountability for accepting updates. Without assessment, organizations auto-update to new versions inheriting unknown changes. This prevents surprise production issues from vendor updates. Essential for vendor dependency management and production stability.

Check:
• Impact assessment required before update acceptance
• Performance, safety, compliance impacts evaluated
• Contractual risk assessment conducted
• Documented approval before production use

Common mistake: Auto-updating third-party models without assessing impacts, causing unexpected production issues.

Ask: Vendor Management/Risk team

Prevents GenAI deployment risks through rigorous prompt engineering governance. Prompts, instructions, guardrails, and retrieval configs control GenAI behavior—they are code and require same rigor. Version control (Git) tracks changes and enables rollback. Independent peer review catches issues before deployment. Safety validation ensures prompts don't enable harmful outputs. Without version control, prompt changes are untracked and irreversible. Peer review prevents single-point-of-failure where one person's prompt mistakes reach production. Essential for GenAI quality and safety assurance.

Check:
• Prompts and configs version-controlled in Git
• Independent peer review required
• Safety validation before deployment
• All GenAI control elements covered

Ask: ML Engineering/GenAI team

Identifies vulnerabilities through comprehensive adversarial testing before they're exploited. Red-teaming attacks systems like real adversaries would—prompt injection, jailbreaks, RAG poisoning, logical contradictions. Testing reveals weaknesses allowing remediation before production. Without testing, vulnerabilities are discovered by malicious actors or users after deployment. Tabletop exercises test procedures and decision-making. Findings must be formally remediated—testing without fixes is pointless. Comprehensive testing across attack vectors ensures broad vulnerability coverage. Essential for GenAI security and safety.

Check:
• Adversarial testing and red-teaming conducted
• Prompt injection and jailbreak testing
• RAG poisoning and contradiction testing
• Findings formally remediated before deployment

Ask: Security/AI Red Team

Ensures reliable decommissioning through automated CI/CD integration. Model teardown and environment destruction in CI/CD means decommissioning is code-based, version-controlled, and repeatable—not manual procedures. Immutable code prevents human error in decommissioning. Automated processes ensure completeness—all components destroyed, no orphaned resources. Manual intervention introduces inconsistency and mistakes. Integration into CI/CD makes decommissioning first-class lifecycle stage with same rigor as deployment. Essential for clean decommissioning preventing security debt from incomplete retirement.

Check:
• Teardown and destruction integrated into CI/CD
• Decommissioning executed via code, not manual
• Version-controlled and repeatable process
• Completeness verification automated

Ask: DevOps/Engineering team

Prevents retirement-related risks through comprehensive decommissioning process. Retiring AI systems without proper process creates security vulnerabilities (orphaned endpoints, active credentials) and operational disruption (downstream dependencies broken). Formal process ensures model artifacts securely deleted (preventing data exposure), downstream dependencies mitigated (preventing cascade failures), and access credentials revoked (preventing posthumous access). Governance approval ensures retirement authorization and impact understanding. Without formal process, retirements are incomplete leaving security and operational debris. Essential for clean system lifecycle completion.

Check:
• Formal retirement process documented
• Model artifacts secure deletion verified
• Downstream dependencies assessed and mitigated
• Access credentials fully revoked

Ask: Governance/Operations team

Manages transparency through formal documentation standards with controlled disclosure. Determining what documentation must be prepared ensures completeness. Defining disclosure categories (users, regulators, auditors) ensures appropriate access. Controlled disclosure procedures prevent unauthorized access to sensitive technical details. Format standards enable consistency. Version control tracks documentation evolution. Access authorization criteria define who can view what. Without formal determination, documentation is ad-hoc and disclosure uncontrolled. Standards enable compliance verification and audit readiness. Essential for systematic transparency management.

Check:
• Documentation requirements formally defined
• Disclosure categories and procedures established
• Format standards and version control
• Access authorization criteria documented

Ask: Governance/Legal team

Ensures audit trail integrity through comprehensive logging requirements with independent verification. Formally defined logging requirements specify what events must be logged across lifecycle. Integrity protection (cryptographic hashing, immutability) prevents tampering. Retention duration defines how long logs are kept. Access controls restrict log viewing. Log completeness ensures no gaps. Periodic independent review validates logging configuration remains effective. Without formal requirements, logging is incomplete or unprotected. Independent review catches logging degradation or gaps. Essential for accountability and forensic capability.

Check:
• Logging requirements formally defined
• Integrity protection and retention specified
• Access controls and completeness requirements
• Periodic independent review conducted

Ask: Security/Compliance team

Establishes comprehensive data governance through formal management processes across lifecycle. AI data management covering all stages ensures consistent treatment from acquisition through disposal. Formally assigned ownership (data stewards, model owners, control functions) creates accountability. Differentiated governance for data types (training, validation, inference, repurposed) applies appropriate controls to each—training data needs different protection than operational data. Without formal process, data management is fragmented and inconsistent. Clear ownership prevents responsibility gaps. Essential for data quality, compliance, and risk management.

Check:
• Formal data management process across all lifecycle stages
• Data ownership formally assigned
• Differentiated governance by data type
• Training, validation, operational, repurposed data covered

Ask: Data Governance team

Prevents problematic data usage through formal acquisition criteria enforced before use. Criteria covering provenance (origin), legal permissibility (lawful to use), licensing (usage rights), privacy (PII protection), and bias (representational fairness) ensure data meets standards. Brokered, synthetic, and third-party datasets require special scrutiny due to opacity. Risk assessment identifies and documents issues before deployment. Without criteria, organizations unknowingly use unlicensed data, biased datasets, or privacy-violating sources. Formal criteria enable consistent evaluation and informed risk acceptance. Essential for data compliance and quality.

Check:
• Acquisition criteria formally defined
• Provenance, legality, licensing, privacy, bias covered
• Third-party and synthetic data explicitly addressed
• Risk assessment required before use

Common mistake: Using data without evaluating licensing, creating copyright violations and legal liability.

Ask: Data Governance/Legal team

Ensures data quality through measurable requirements with automated validation. Defining requirements (accuracy, completeness, representativeness, bias thresholds) establishes standards. Validation mechanisms verify data meets requirements before use—automated checks prevent bad data from entering pipelines. Formal escalation process addresses failures—who is notified, what actions taken when data fails checks. Without requirements and validation, poor quality data trains unreliable models. Escalation ensures quality failures are addressed not ignored. Measurable standards enable objective assessment. Essential for model quality and reliability.

Check:
• Data quality requirements formally defined
• Validation mechanisms verify thresholds
• Automated checks before data use
• Formal escalation process for failures

Ask: Data Governance/Engineering team

Enables data accountability through technically enforced provenance tracking across lifecycle. Recording origin, transformations, labeling, preprocessing, versions, and usage creates complete data lineage. Technical enforcement through system logging, metadata tagging, or lineage tools ensures tracking happens automatically—not relying on manual documentation that's incomplete or outdated. Provenance enables debugging (what data caused this issue), compliance verification (was this data properly licensed), and reproducibility (exact data used for training). Without automated tracking, provenance degrades as data flows through pipelines. Essential for data accountability and auditability.

Check:
• Provenance tracking across full lifecycle
• Origin, transformations, labeling, versions tracked
• Technical enforcement via logging/metadata/lineage tools
• Automated, not manual documentation

Ask: Data Engineering/Governance team

Prevents data preparation issues through formal criteria with reproducibility capability. Defining preparation methods criteria ensures consistent processing. Evaluating for unintended impacts (bias amplification during aggregation, privacy risk from joining datasets) catches issues early. Documented reproducibility means preparation pipeline can be reconstructed—critical for model retraining or audit. Without criteria, data preparation is ad-hoc and unreproducible. Impact evaluation catches hidden risks. Reproducibility enables validation and debugging. Essential for data quality and governance.

Check:
• Formal criteria for preparation methods
• Preparation evaluated for bias/privacy impacts
• Reproducibility capability documented
• Pipeline reconstruction possible for audit

Ask: Data Engineering/Governance team

Applies proportionate controls through risk-based data classification. Classification framework categorizes datasets by sensitivity (PII, confidential, public) and criticality (business impact). Controls (access restriction, encryption, masking, monitoring) applied proportionally to classification—highly sensitive data gets strongest protection. Without classification, all data treated equally (wasteful) or critical data under-protected (dangerous). Risk-based approach allocates security resources efficiently. Classification enables compliance (GDPR requires extra protection for sensitive data). Essential for data security and regulatory compliance.

Check:
• Formal data classification framework established
• Sensitivity and risk criticality assessed
• Controls proportional to classification level
• Access, encryption, masking, monitoring applied

Ask: Data Governance/Security team

Protects training data integrity through poisoning detection and prevention. Data poisoning attacks inject malicious examples subtly altering model behavior. Multimodal adversarial payloads (steganography hiding malicious data in images) bypass simple checks. Technical controls use anomaly detection identifying unusual patterns. Automated blocking prevents poisoned batches from entering training. Procedural controls add human review for high-risk scenarios. Without controls, attackers can manipulate model behavior through training data. Essential for training data security and model integrity.

Check:
• Data poisoning detection controls implemented
• Multimodal adversarial payload detection
• Anomaly detection and automated blocking
• Outlier batch identification

Ask: Security/Data Engineering team

Manages synthetic data risks through formal governance covering generation through deployment. Synthetic/LLM-generated data can inherit biases, have unrealistic distributions, or lack critical edge cases. Formal documentation of generation methods enables assessment. Risk assessment identifies quality, bias, or privacy issues. Quality validation ensures synthetic data is appropriate for intended use. Ask: Data Science/Governance team

Ensures compliant data retention through documented policy with enforcement. Retention policy defines how long datasets are kept for defined purposes. Check:
• Dataset retention policy documented
• Secure archival and deletion procedures defined

• Policy enforcement mechanisms in place

Ask: Data Governance/Legal team

Prevents ungoverned data through shadow dataset detection and remediation. Shadow datasets exist outside formal registration—used by teams but unknown to governance. • Retrospective registration process defined

Ask: Data Governance/Security team

Without adversarial testing, monitoring might catch simple drift but miss coordinated attacks. Sensitivity testing reveals detection thresholds; response time testing validates intervention speed. Check:
• Adversarial drift scenarios actively simulated
• Slow-burn poisoning and coordinated shifts tested
• Monitoring sensitivity assessed
• Response time validation conducted

Ask: Security/ML Engineering team

Prevents retraining disasters through automated quality gates halting deployment. Catastrophic forgetting (model loses previously learned capabilities during retraining), severe performance degradation, or newly introduced bias can occur during retraining. • Automated circuit breakers in retraining pipeline

• Performance degradation and bias detection
• Tolerance thresholds predefined

Ask: ML Engineering/DevOps team

Ask: Legal/Data Privacy team

• Annotator error rates evaluated
• Labeling bias mitigation processes

Ask: ML Operations/Data team

Assesses third-party model training data risks through comprehensive evaluation before use. Risk assessment identifies these issues enabling informed decisions. Declared limitations documentation sets expectations. Without assessment, organizations deploy models with unknown inherited risks. Training data assessment is critical—model behavior reflects training data quality and biases. Essential for third-party model risk management.

Check:
• Training data risk assessment conducted
• Lineage, provenance, representativeness evaluated
• Contamination, PII, copyright exposure assessed
• Training data limitations declared and documented

Ask: Risk Management/Legal team

Addresses data subject rights challenges in AI context through formal impact assessment. Check:
• Data subject rights impact formally assessed
• Training dataset and retraining implications documented
• Technical feasibility of data removal evaluated
• Assessment reviewed when regulations/architectures change

Ask: Data Privacy/Legal team

Lawful basis requirements (GDPR legal basis for processing) and cross-border transfer obligations must be satisfied. Without assessment, organizations violate privacy laws by using data beyond original authorized purposes. Essential for compliant AI training data sourcing.

Check:
• Purpose compatibility formally assessed
• Explicit consent and lawful basis verified
• Cross-border transfer obligations evaluated
• Assessment for all repurposed data

• Sufficient detail for investigation

Ask: Security/Data Governance team

Ensures apprenticeship and mentorship systems remain functional when AI eliminates traditional learning mechanisms. Senior professionals historically trained juniors through work delegation and review; automation removes this interaction destroying knowledge transfer and culture transmission.

Check:
• Mentorship programs redesigned for AI-augmented work
• Knowledge transfer mechanisms beyond work delegation
• Senior-junior interaction preserved despite automation
• Cultural values transmission protected

Common mistake: AI eliminating work delegation removes all senior-junior interaction, severing mentorship relationships, and destroying organizational culture and tacit knowledge transfer.

Ask: Practice Leaders, Professional Development, Partnership Committee

Defines new professional identity and value proposition when AI performs traditional core work. Professionals derive meaning and status from expertise AI now demonstrates; organizations must articulate why human professionals remain valuable preventing existential career crisis.

Check:
• Professional value proposition redefined for AI era
• Clear articulation of uniquely human contributions
• Career meaning and purpose addressed explicitly
• Professional identity supported through transition

Common mistake: Deploying AI that performs "professional work" without articulating new professional value proposition, causing identity crisis, demoralization, and exodus of talented professionals.

Ask: Executive Leadership, Practice Leaders, Professional Development

Prevents "paving the cow path" by automating broken processes with AI rather than redesigning for efficiency. AI deployment on inefficient workflows locks in waste at machine speed; process redesign before automation eliminates root inefficiencies first.

Check:
• Process mapping completed before AI deployment
• Bottlenecks and inefficiencies identified and addressed
• Workflow redesigned for human-AI collaboration
• Business case validates automation targets right processes

Common mistake: Automating existing manual workflows without questioning whether process itself is optimal, achieving efficiency gains while missing transformation opportunities.

Ask: Process Excellence Team, Operations Team, Department Managers

Defines clear decision authority allocation preventing confusion, bottlenecks, and accountability gaps. Without explicit rules specifying which decisions AI makes autonomously versus requiring human approval, processes stall in approval loops or proceed unsafely on autopilot.

Check:
• Decision rights matrix documented (AI autonomous, AI recommends, human decides)
• Authority levels aligned with risk and complexity
• Override protocols established and communicated
• Accountability assignment clear for each decision type

Common mistake: Deploying AI without defining decision authority, creating organizational paralysis as humans await AI or AI awaits humans with no clarity on who decides.

Ask: Process Owners, Legal Team, Risk Management

Establishes exception handling protocols for cases AI cannot process autonomously. Without defined escalation paths, exceptions create bottlenecks, AI systems freeze awaiting human intervention, or worse, AI proceeds incorrectly rather than requesting help.

Check:
• Exception criteria documented (what triggers escalation)
• Escalation paths and response times defined
• Human expert availability ensured
• Exception logs tracked for process improvement

Common mistake: AI handles 95% of cases efficiently but 5% exceptions create chaos with no routing mechanism, causing delays exceeding pre-AI processing times.

Ask: Operations Team, IT Team, Process Owners

Ensures quality assurance mechanisms exist for AI outputs preventing error propagation through downstream processes. Humans must validate AI work without becoming rubber-stamps; effective QA requires sampling strategies, validation criteria, and error feedback loops.

Check:
• AI output validation requirements defined
• Sampling strategy for QA (not 100% review, not 0%)
• Validation criteria and error thresholds established
• Feedback loops from QA to AI model improvement

Common mistake: Either humans review 100% of AI outputs negating efficiency gains, or review 0% accepting all AI outputs allowing errors to compound downstream.

Ask: Quality Assurance Team, Process Owners, Risk Management

Optimizes approval workflows preventing AI recommendations from stalling in endless human review cycles. AI can generate recommendations quickly but value is lost if approvals take weeks; streamlined authority and risk-based routing enable speed without sacrificing control.

Check:
• Approval requirements tiered by risk/impact
• Approval authorities empowered to act quickly
• Approval SLAs defined and monitored
• Bottleneck analysis identifies approval delays

Common mistake: AI reduces analysis time from 5 days to 5 hours but approvals still take 2 weeks, negating 95% of AI time savings through organizational friction.

Ask: Process Excellence Team, Department Leaders, Change Management

Updates process documentation reflecting hybrid human-AI workflows enabling training, compliance, and audit. Documentation built for 100% human execution becomes obsolete and misleading; updated materials must specify AI roles, handoffs, and human responsibilities.

Check:
• Process documentation updated for AI integration
• Roles and responsibilities clearly assigned (human vs AI)
• Handoff points and data flows documented
• Version control maintains current documentation

Common mistake: Maintaining pre-AI process documentation causing new employees to be trained on obsolete workflows, auditors to review wrong processes, and compliance to be assessed incorrectly.

Ask: Process Documentation Team, Training Team, Compliance Team

Establishes change management protocols for ongoing process evolution as AI capabilities improve. AI systems update frequently changing what they can automate; processes must evolve dynamically requiring continuous change management rather than one-time transformation.

Check:
• Process change governance established
• Impact assessment required for AI capability changes
• Communication protocols for process updates
• Training provided when processes change

Common mistake: Treating AI deployment as one-time change, discovering processes must evolve quarterly as AI improves but lacking change management infrastructure for continuous transformation.

Ask: Change Management Team, IT Governance, Process Owners

Ensures audit trails and compliance evidence capture for hybrid human-AI processes. Regulators and auditors require documentation of who made decisions and why; AI decision-making creates new compliance requirements for explainability, bias detection, and human oversight evidence.

Check:
• Audit logging captures both human and AI decisions
• Decision rationale recorded (AI reasoning + human overrides)
• Compliance evidence meets regulatory requirements
• Audit trail retention aligned with regulations

Common mistake: Audit systems designed for human decisions fail to capture AI decision-making, creating compliance gaps discovered during regulatory examination.

Ask: Compliance Team, Internal Audit, Legal Team

Defines performance metrics measuring hybrid process effectiveness rather than just speed or cost. Traditional metrics (cycle time, unit cost) miss quality degradation, employee satisfaction, or customer experience changes; balanced scorecards capture AI transformation holistically.

Check:
• Performance metrics updated for hybrid workflows
• Quality, satisfaction, and outcome metrics included
• Balanced scorecard approach prevents optimization myopia
• Metrics tracked over time identifying trends

Common mistake: Measuring only efficiency gains (30% faster, 20% cheaper) while missing quality drops, employee burnout, or customer dissatisfaction destroying long-term value.

Ask: Performance Management Team, Finance Team, Operations Team

Establishes continuous improvement mechanisms capturing learnings from human-AI collaboration for process optimization. AI deployments generate data on failures, exceptions, and edge cases; systematic analysis converts experience into process improvements and AI training enhancements.

Check:
• Process improvement governance established
• Exception analysis drives optimization
• Human feedback captured and analyzed
• Continuous improvement culture maintained

Common mistake: Deploying AI then running processes unchanged for years, missing opportunities to optimize based on accumulated operational experience and changing business needs.

Ask: Process Excellence Team, Continuous Improvement Team, Operations Leaders

Identifies institutional knowledge being transferred into AI systems preventing unintentional IP externalization. Organizations train AI on historical decisions, expert judgment patterns, and proprietary processes without realizing this knowledge becomes embedded in vendor-owned models outside institutional control.

Check:
• Knowledge inventory completed before AI training
• Proprietary methodologies and expertise identified
• Competitive advantages and strategic knowledge catalogued
• Knowledge transfer assessment for each AI use case

Common mistake: Training AI on decades of institutional expertise (clinical decisions, manufacturing optimization, policy analysis) without documenting what knowledge AI is learning, discovering later that organizational IP is embedded in vendor systems.

Ask: Knowledge Management Team, Legal Team, Strategic Planning

Ensures institutional ownership of knowledge embedded in trained AI models preventing permanent IP loss. Without explicit contractual terms, vendors typically own trained models including institutional expertise learned during training; when vendor relationship ends, institution loses access to its own knowledge.

Check:
• Contracts specify institution owns trained models and embedded knowledge
• IP assignment clauses reviewed by legal counsel
• Model weights and parameters accessible to institution
• Knowledge extraction rights documented if vendor acquired

Common mistake: Signing vendor contracts with standard terms giving vendor ownership of trained models, discovering hospital clinical expertise, manufacturing processes, or policy methodologies are now vendor IP inaccessible after contract termination.

Ask: Legal Team, Procurement, Contracts Team, Chief IP Officer

Maintains independent documentation of institutional knowledge outside AI systems ensuring recovery capability when AI unavailable. Relying exclusively on AI to store expertise creates catastrophic failure mode: vendor bankruptcy, service termination, or relationship end results in permanent institutional knowledge loss.

Check:
• Knowledge documented independently of AI systems
• Expert methodologies recorded in accessible formats
• Standard operating procedures maintained outside vendor platforms
• Institutional memory preserved beyond AI embeddings

Common mistake: Senior experts retire after training AI on their expertise without documenting knowledge independently, AI vendor goes bankrupt, institution permanently loses decades of manufacturing optimization, clinical judgment, or operational expertise.

Ask: Knowledge Management Team, Documentation Team, Operations

Establishes knowledge recovery and exit strategy preventing operational paralysis from vendor dependency. Without extraction mechanisms, institutional expertise embedded in AI becomes permanently inaccessible when vendor relationships end, creating business continuity crisis as critical operations depend on unavailable knowledge.

Check:
• Knowledge extraction procedures documented and tested
• Model export capabilities verified in contracts
• Data portability mechanisms established
• Alternative vendor migration paths identified

Common mistake: Operating for years with critical functions dependent on vendor AI without exit strategy, vendor acquired by competitor or demands 500% price increase, discovering institution cannot extract embedded knowledge or migrate to alternatives.

Ask: IT Governance, Business Continuity Team, Vendor Management

Classifies strategic institutional knowledge requiring enhanced protection preventing competitive or national security exposure. Not all knowledge has equal value; strategic expertise (competitive advantages, national security methodologies, breakthrough research) transferred to AI creates unacceptable risk if exposed through vendor breach, acquisition, or foreign access.

Check:
• Strategic knowledge classification scheme established
• Competitive advantage and national security knowledge identified
• Enhanced protections for strategic knowledge in AI training
• Vendor security and jurisdiction assessed for strategic knowledge

Common mistake: Training AI indiscriminately on all institutional data including strategic decision-making patterns, trading strategies, or defense analysis methodologies, vendor gets acquired by competitor or foreign entity gaining access to institution's most valuable knowledge.

Ask: Strategic Planning, Chief Security Officer, Risk Management, Legal

Identifies critical institutional functions dependent on third-party AI preventing operational blindness to vendor dependency. Without systematic inventory, organizations discover too late that core operations cannot function without vendor AI creating catastrophic failure mode during vendor bankruptcy, service outage, or relationship termination.

Check:
• Critical function inventory mapping AI dependencies
• Business impact analysis for each AI-dependent function
• Operational criticality ratings assigned
• Dependency documentation maintained and reviewed quarterly

Common mistake: AI adoption spreads organically across departments without central tracking, discovering during vendor crisis that customer service, clinical operations, financial processing, or supply chain management cannot operate without unavailable vendor AI.

Ask: Enterprise Architecture, IT Governance, Operations Team, Risk Management

Assesses vendor concentration risk preventing single point of failure catastrophe. Dependency on single AI vendor for multiple critical functions creates extreme vulnerability: vendor failure, acquisition by competitor, or service degradation simultaneously disables numerous operations with no alternative provider.

Check:
• Vendor concentration analysis performed
• Single vendor dependency thresholds established
• Multi-vendor strategy for critical functions
• Contingency plans for dominant vendor failure

Common mistake: Multiple departments independently selecting same AI vendor creating unintended concentration, discovering 80% of critical operations depend on single vendor when vendor demands 400% price increase, gets acquired by competitor, or experiences multi-day outage.

Ask: Vendor Management, Procurement, Enterprise Risk Management, CIO

Quantifies exit barriers and switching costs preventing vendor lock-in trap. Without documented exit analysis, organizations negotiate contracts unaware of future dependency, discovering years later that switching costs ($10M-$500M+), migration timelines (12-36 months), and business disruption make exit economically impossible creating permanent vendor hostage situation.

Check:
• Exit cost analysis completed before vendor selection
• Data portability and migration mechanisms verified
• Switching timeline and business disruption assessed
• Alternative vendor compatibility validated

Common mistake: Implementing enterprise AI without exit planning, operating 5-10 years with deepening dependency, vendor demands massive price increases or degrades service, discovering migration would cost $100M+ and risk operational collapse forcing acceptance of any vendor terms.

Ask: Finance Team, IT Architecture, Vendor Management, Business Continuity

Establishes contractual protections and leverage preventing vendor exploitation of dependency. Once deeply dependent, organizations have zero negotiating power unless contracts include price caps, service level guarantees, change-of-control provisions, and termination rights; without protections, vendors can unilaterally raise prices, degrade service, or change terms.

Check:
• Price escalation caps in multi-year contracts
• Service level agreements with penalties for violations
• Change-of-control clauses protecting against acquisitions
• Termination rights preserving exit options

Common mistake: Signing standard vendor contracts without dependency protections, years later vendor raises prices 300%, reduces support quality, or gets acquired by competitor, contract provides no recourse forcing acceptance of exploitative terms or catastrophic exit.

Ask: Legal Team, Procurement, Contracts Management, Finance

Maintains operational continuity capability during third-party AI outages preventing complete business paralysis. Without manual fallback procedures, tested backup systems, or alternative processing capability, vendor service disruptions (outages, cyber attacks, bankruptcies) cause immediate operational collapse as AI-dependent functions have no contingency mode.

Check:
• Manual fallback procedures documented for AI-dependent functions
• Backup systems or alternative vendors identified
• Business continuity plans tested including AI unavailability scenarios
• Staff trained to operate without AI during emergencies

Common mistake: Critical operations (hospital patient care, financial trading, customer service, supply chain) completely dependent on vendor AI with no fallback capability, vendor experiences multi-day outage or bankruptcy, operations stop entirely causing patient harm, financial losses, or customer abandonment.

Ask: Business Continuity Planning, Operations Team, IT Disaster Recovery, Risk Management

Maps foreign technology dependencies in critical institutional functions preventing geopolitical vulnerability blindness. Organizations deploy AI without tracking geographic origin of vendors, infrastructure, or data flows, discovering during international tensions that strategic operations depend on foreign powers creating leverage, sanctions exposure, or service cutoff risk.

Check:
• Geographic origin analysis for all AI vendors and infrastructure
• Critical function mapping to vendor nationality and jurisdiction
• Foreign dependency assessment for strategic operations
• Geopolitical risk evaluation for each dependency

Common mistake: Hospital, government agency, or critical infrastructure deploys AI systems without assessing vendor nationality, data jurisdiction, or geopolitical exposure, discovering during international crisis that foreign-controlled AI manages critical functions creating strategic vulnerability.

Ask: Risk Management, Strategic Planning, National Security Office, CIO

Ensures data sovereignty and jurisdictional control preventing sensitive institutional data from flowing to foreign jurisdictions with different legal frameworks, surveillance laws, or adversarial intelligence services. Data stored or processed in foreign countries subjects institution to foreign government access, legal compulsion, or intelligence exploitation.

Check:
• Data residency requirements established for sensitive data
• Physical storage locations verified and monitored
• Processing jurisdictions for AI computations documented
• Foreign government access risks assessed and mitigated

Common mistake: Healthcare system, financial institution, or government agency trains AI on sensitive data without verifying storage location, data flows to foreign cloud servers subject to foreign surveillance laws, adversarial intelligence services gain access to patient records, financial transactions, or classified information.

Ask: Privacy Officer, Legal Team, Data Protection Officer, National Security

Assesses geopolitical resilience and operational continuity if foreign AI services are denied through sanctions, export controls, diplomatic tensions, or trade restrictions. International relations can deteriorate rapidly; institutions dependent on foreign AI face operational collapse if access is revoked for geopolitical reasons beyond their control.

Check:
• Scenarios for foreign AI service denial developed
• Operational impact if foreign vendors cut off assessed
• Alternative domestic or allied-nation sources identified
• Continuity plans for geopolitical service disruptions

Common mistake: European hospitals depend entirely on US AI diagnostics, US-China trade war escalates with AI export controls, European nations forced to choose geopolitical alignment, healthcare operations held hostage to international politics with no domestic alternatives, patient care disrupted by geopolitics.

Ask: Strategic Planning, Business Continuity, Risk Management, Government Relations

Validates technology sovereignty and domestic capability development preventing permanent foreign dependency trap. Without domestic AI alternatives, institutions and nations become permanently subject to foreign technology providers with no sovereign capability for strategic independence, creating multi-generational vulnerability and digital colonialism.

Check:
• Technology sovereignty strategy defined
• Domestic AI capability assessment and development roadmap
• Investment in sovereign alternatives for critical functions
• Partnerships with allied nations for technology independence

Common mistake: Developing nation builds entire digital economy on foreign Big Tech AI with no domestic capability investment, foreign providers raise prices 10x or impose exploitative terms, nation has zero alternatives creating permanent technological colonialism and strategic subordination.

Ask: Strategic Planning, National Technology Policy, Economic Development, Innovation Office

Secures AI supply chain against foreign adversary compromise preventing backdoors, kill switches, or malicious functionality in AI systems from adversarial sources. Foreign components in AI infrastructure (chips, software libraries, training data, cloud services) create attack vectors for supply chain compromise enabling surveillance, sabotage, or remote disablement during conflict.

Check:
• AI supply chain mapped including all foreign components
• Adversarial nation components identified and assessed
• Trusted supply chain requirements for critical AI systems
• Validation and testing for backdoors or malicious functionality

Common mistake: Military or critical infrastructure deploys AI with components from adversarial nations (chips, code libraries, cloud services) without supply chain security, during geopolitical conflict adversaries activate backdoors disabling weapons systems, power grids, or communications infrastructure through pre-positioned supply chain compromises.
